# Ballot Book NZ: the 2026 election report

**New Zealand general election: Saturday 7 November 2026.** Snapshot taken **23 October 2026**. Advance voting opens on Monday 26 October,
and the last day to enrol is Sunday 25 October. There is no election-day enrolment this year
([elections/2026.md](elections/2026.md); [Electoral Commission factsheet](https://elections.nz/assets/2026-General-Election/2026-Factsheet-Make-Sure-Youre-Enrolled-for-the-2026-General-Election-v2.pdf)).

This report pulls together the whole archive: results since 2008, 129 polls taken since the 2023 election, about 1,400 policy
statements for 2026, and promise-by-promise track records for eight parties. It describes the parties and their records. It
**does not recommend any party**. Each factual sentence links to an outside source or to the archive file it comes from, and
those files carry their own sources. Tables marked `GENERATED` are built from the JSON by
[`tools/report_stats.py`](tools/report_stats.py), so the numbers match the data. Run `python3 tools/report_stats.py --write`
to rebuild them.

**Contents:** [1. Summary](#1-summary-for-busy-voters) · [2. The parties](#2-the-2026-choice-party-by-party) ·
[3. Head-to-head](#3-head-to-head-on-the-big-issues) · [4. Promise-keeping](#4-reliability-and-promise-keeping) ·
[5. Performance in government](#5-performance-in-government-200826) · [6. Trends](#6-trends-20112026) ·
[7. Who's who](#7-whos-who) · [8. Data quality](#8-data-quality-and-limitations) · [9. Using the archive](#9-how-to-use-this-archive)

---

## 1. Summary for busy voters

**The state of play.** The 2023 election produced New Zealand's first three-party coalition under MMP: National, ACT and NZ
First, led by Christopher Luxon. It started with 68 of 123 seats ([data/elections/2023.json](data/elections/2023.json);
[data/parliaments/54.json](data/parliaments/54.json)). Over the term National's vote has slid from 38% to the high 20s, NZ First and TOP
have risen, and the Greens have reached record poll levels. The polls now show a race too close to call
([elections/2026.md](elections/2026.md#polling)).

**What those numbers could mean in seats.** The table below applies the Sainte-Laguë formula to the 30-day poll average. It uses
the same seat rules as the Electoral Act: a party needs 5% of the party vote or one electorate seat, and the House can grow if a
party wins overhang seats ([trends §3](elections/trends.md#3-turnout-overhang-and-the-wasted-vote)). It is an illustration, not a
forecast. Polls carry sampling error of roughly ±3 points for a party near 30%, and TOP is close enough to 5% that small movements
change the result.

- unemployment, 19%.

### 2.1 National (centre-right) – leader Christopher Luxon

- **Stands for:** National leads the current government. It wants taxes kept where they are, spending held tight and the books
  back in surplus ([guide card](data/guide/parties.json); [Wikipedia label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party)).
- **Headline 2026 policies:** the "ten commitments" launched on 27 September 2026 ([National](https://www.national.org.nz/news/260927-christopherluxon-1)):
  - no new taxes;
  - compulsory KiwiSaver, with a $1,500 "Baby Boost";
  - paid parental leave extended from 26 to 30 weeks;
  - replace NCEA;
  - wider 5%-deposit First Home Loans;
  - structural separation of Foodstuffs;
  - $604m more for Pharmac and free bowel screening from 50, part-funded by cutting non-Pacific aid;
  - drug-testing of some beneficiaries;
  - no "good character" discounts in sentencing for sex offending;
  - referendums on MMP and on a four-year term.

  Sources: [README](parties/national/README.md#the-2026-campaign-pitch-and-headline-promises); [all 159 policies](parties/national/policies/README.md).
- **Costings:** its fiscal plan (12 Oct 2026) keeps new spending to $2.4b a year and leaves $7.5b unallocated over four years
  ([fiscal plan PDF](https://assets.national.org.nz/web/prod/National's%20Fiscal%20Plan.pdf)). It targets an OBEGALx surplus in 2028/29
  and debt below 40% of GDP ([README](parties/national/README.md)).
- **They say:** "Fixing the Basics, Building the Future"; it will "not impose new taxes". **Critics say:** Labour says "unemployment is
  higher, growth is weaker, debt has continued to rise" ([Labour fiscal plan](https://www.labour.org.nz/fiscal-plan)).
- **Coalition:** wants to continue with ACT and NZ First; rules out Labour and TOP (see §1).
- **Track record:** 61 resolved promises, delivery index 66% (§4). It kept most of its repeal and legislation promises and
  missed more of its outcome targets: the surplus date, 500 police, fees-free and the Dunedin Hospital
  ([track-record.md](parties/national/track-record.md#summary)).

### 2.2 Labour (centre-left) – leader Chris Hipkins

- **Stands for:** Labour is the main opposition and governed from 2017 to 2023. It is campaigning on health costs paid for by a new
  property tax, and on taking on big companies over prices ([guide card](data/guide/parties.json)).
- **Headline 2026 policies** ("Better Starts Now") ([README](parties/labour/README.md#2026-pitch-and-headline-promises); [126 policies](parties/labour/policies/README.md)):
  - a 28% capital gains tax on residential and commercial property (excluding the family home and farms) to fund up to three free
    GP visits a year;
  - free prescriptions, free cervical screening and free maternity scans;
  - restore the old pay-equity law, with a $4/hour pay rise for 65,000 care workers;
  - make price gouging illegal and force supermarkets to separate wholesale from retail;
  - $20/week public transport fare caps in the three biggest cities;
  - a 10% student-loan write-off;
  - at least 6,000 social homes;
  - a "NZ Future Fund";
  - repeal the Regulatory Standards Act within 100 days.
- **Costings:** its fiscal plan (Oct 2026) was reviewed by Hall Chadwick. It keeps the $2.4b operating allowance, forecasts a surplus
  in 2028/29 and targets net debt below 20% of GDP ([Labour](https://www.labour.org.nz/fiscal-plan)). National's Nicola Willis says
  restoring pay equity alone would cost $11b on Treasury estimates ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1733687/labour-s-fiscal-plan-national-s-claims-and-how-labour-is-defending-it)).
  Economists have queried the fare-cap costing: Labour says $65m, their estimates are $91–112m ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/598268/material-miscalculation-economists-identify-apparent-errors-in-labour-s-transport-policy)).
  Labour will not publish Future Fund costings before the election ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-admits-it-will-not-release-cornerstone-policy-costing-and-job-modelling-until-after-the-election-blames-treaty-of-waitangi-concerns/QNGXJK4SHZFOJB52WFCVHPLR4E/)).
- **Coalition:** will govern with the Greens and is open to TOP and (with limits) Te Pāti Māori. It rules out NZ First and ACT.
  Hipkins has ruled out giving the Greens or Te Pāti Māori the police or corrections portfolios
  ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2026-labours-chris-hipkins-rules-out-greens-te-pati-maori-from-major-ministerial-roles-in-herald-debate/3GBPYMI6TJBKHLVNOSPGY6WTKA/)).
- **Campaign note (23 Oct 2026):** Labour's Tāmaki Makaurau candidate Kerrin Leoni resigned as a candidate after footage showed her
  campaigning at a gathering attended by Mongrel Mob members; Hipkins called it "inconsistent with the standards I expect of Labour
  candidates". Her name stays on the ballot because nominations had closed
  ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/10/23/labours-leoni-resigns-after-gang-campaigning-video-emerges/)).
- **Track record:** 61 scored promises from 2017–23, delivery index 67%. It reliably delivered laws and money transfers (about 71%
  kept outright) but kept only 2 of 13 big build or outcome targets outright (KiwiBuild, light rail, the migration cut)
  ([track-record.md](parties/labour/track-record.md#6-reliability-scorecard)). If Labour wins, the CGT will be its key test: the
  party has promised and then dropped a CGT four times since 2011 ([track-record §9](parties/labour/track-record.md#9-what-the-record-suggests-for-2026-promises)).

### 2.3 Green Party (centre-left to left-wing) – co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick

- **Stands for:** strong climate and nature action, and a higher income floor paid for by taxing the very wealthy
  ([guide card](data/guide/parties.json); [Charter](parties/green/README.md#3-values-the-charter)).
- **Headline 2026 policies** ("For All of Us") ([README §10](parties/green/README.md#10-2026-pitch-and-headline-promises); [564 itemised policies](parties/green/policies/README.md)):
  - tax:
    - a 2.5% wealth tax on net wealth over $10m;
    - an inheritance and gift tax;
    - a 33% rate for the biggest companies;
    - a new top bracket above $160,000;
    - the first $10,000 of income tax-free;
  - housing: a 2% cap on rent rises and many more public homes;
  - "KiwiMart", a state supermarket chain made up of 120 stores the big two would have to sell;
  - "Kiwipower", a public renewable-energy company;
  - $2 public transport fares;
  - repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act and revoke the mining consents granted under it;
  - restore pay equity and free school lunches.
- **Costings:** its fiscal plan (23 Oct 2026) had its direct effects reviewed by Infometrics. It raises about $28.75b over four years
  from new taxes, delays surplus to 2029/30 and has net core Crown debt at 44% of GDP by 2030/31
  ([Newstalk ZB](https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/election-2026-green-party-s-plan-to-transform-nz-s-finances-with-more-tax-spending-debt/);
  [B2B News](https://b2bnews.co.nz/news/greens-fiscal-plan-adds-26-point-6bn-in-debt-by-2030-31/)). The plan document itself could
  not be retrieved ([policies README](parties/green/policies/README.md)). National says it contains "nine new taxes" (same source).
- **Coalition:** will support only a Labour-led government. It has not formally ruled any party in or out
  ([README §11](parties/green/README.md#11-coalition-stance)).
- **Track record:** the Greens have never been in Cabinet. They were a support partner from 2017 to 2023. Delivery index 59% overall,
  67% as a support partner. Delivery was best in 2017–20, when Labour needed their votes. Two breaches of the party's own stated
  principles are recorded: the 2018 waka-jumping vote and the 2020 Green School grant
  ([track-record.md](parties/green/track-record.md#1-scorecard)).

### 2.4 ACT (right-wing) – leader David Seymour

- **Stands for:** a smaller state, lower spending, deregulation, and "one law for all" regardless of race
  ([README](parties/act/README.md); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_New_Zealand)).
- **Headline 2026 policies** ([110 policies](parties/act/policies/README.md); [guide card](data/guide/parties.json)):
  - merge 43 departments into 19 and abolish population-group ministries;
  - raise the super age gradually to 67 by 2035;
  - repeal the Zero Carbon Act and abolish the Climate Change Commission;
  - a three-year minimum-wage freeze and a training wage;
  - three strikes for burglary;
  - deport serious non-citizen offenders;
  - close the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are settled;
  - opposes breaking up the supermarkets.
- **Costings:** its fiscal plan (11 Oct 2026) promises lower debt and spending, including $653m less on disability benefits
  ([ACT fiscal plan PDF](https://assets.nationbuilder.com/actnz/pages/38747/attachments/original/1791599898/ACT_2026_Fiscal_Plan.pdf?1791599898)).
  RNZ noted two unexplained items, one of about $100m a year and one of $264–303m a year of tax relief
  ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1835030/election-2026-as-it-happened-11-oct-greens-label-act-fiscal-plan-welfare-for-the-wealthiest-opportunity-seeks-answers-over-assumptions)).
  The Greens call the plan "welfare for the wealthiest" (same source).
- **Coalition:** wants to "lock Labour out" and is open to a four-party deal that includes TOP
  ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1932454/four-headed-beast-act-leader-david-seymour-hints-at-potential-for-coalition-with-opportunity)).
- **Track record:** delivery index 61% overall and 64% for 2023–26. Its track record calls ACT "highly reliable at delivering what it
  negotiates, but negotiated away a good part of what it campaigned on". Examples it traded away: the Treaty referendum, its own tax
  plan, and repeal of the Zero Carbon Act ([track-record.md](parties/act/track-record.md#reliability-scorecard)).

### 2.5 NZ First (Wikipedia gives no infobox label; its opening sentence says "right-wing populist") – leader Winston Peters

- **Stands for:** "citizens first" policy, seniors and the regions, opposition to what it calls "co-governance" (shared Māori–Crown
  decision-making arrangements), and state intervention in the economy such as breaking up big companies ([README](parties/nz-first/README.md); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First)).
- **Headline 2026 policies** ([79 policies](parties/nz-first/policies/README.md)):
  - split the "gentailer" power companies;
  - split Foodstuffs into two cooperatives;
  - buy back BNZ and merge it with Kiwibank;
  - only citizens could vote or receive NZ Super;
  - a $5,000-a-year "Kiwi Kids Grant";
  - a 20% company tax rate for small and medium businesses;
  - binding referendums on the Māori seats and on capping resident visas;
  - repeal the Regulatory Standards Act it voted for.
- **Costings:** no full fiscal plan. The NZ Herald calls it the largest party in Parliament not to publish one
  ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/nz-firsts-policies-could-cost-72b-and-that-doesnt-include-buying-back-the-bnz/premium/SMEMEEW25JE7DC4IQPTINQGFYA/)).
  A Green Party analysis puts its policies at about $71.6b over four years, which NZ First rejects without giving its own figures.
  Estimates of the cost of buying BNZ range from NZ First's own $7.5b to $24b (the Herald does not name the source of the higher
  figure) (same source, 22 Oct 2026).
- **Coalition:** National and ACT only; rules out Labour and will not sit in Cabinet with TOP's leader (see §1).
- **Track record:** delivery index 56% overall. The pattern: what gets into a coalition agreement is usually delivered (the PGF, the
  RIF, keeping super at 65), while the most divisive campaign promises are often traded away and then revived at the next election
  ([track-record.md](parties/nz-first/track-record.md#reliability-scorecard)).

### 2.6 The Opportunity Party (TOP) (centre) – leader Qiulae Wong

- **Stands for:** policies it describes as evidence-based; Wikipedia and policy.nz label it "radical centrist". TOP has never been in Parliament
  ([README](parties/opportunity/README.md); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_Party_(New_Zealand))).
- **Headline 2026 policies** ([77 policies](parties/opportunity/policies/README.md)):
  - a means-tested Citizen's Income of up to $370 a week for most adults, replacing most benefits and NZ Super, funded by a land value tax;
  - a $30,000 donation cap, a lobbying register and an anti-corruption watchdog;
  - a 10-year health plan, with health funding at 9% of GDP;
  - a ban on inshore bottom trawling by 2030;
  - stronger Commerce Commission powers;
  - farming brought into the ETS.

  Its five "non-negotiables" were set out on 30 September ([README](parties/opportunity/README.md#2026-campaign-summary)).
- **Costings:** no full fiscal plan. Its "Tax Reset" says the land tax pays for the Citizen's Income with about $4b a year to spare
  ([TOP PDF](https://cdn.opportunity.org.nz/documents/policy/Opportunity%20Policy%20-%20Tax%20Reset.pdf)). The commentator Grant Duncan argues that
  surplus is largely offset by new borrowing costs ([Substack](https://grantduncanphd.substack.com/p/opportunity-what-does-top-really)).
- **Coalition:** open to either side, but not to a government with Peters as Foreign Minister (see §1).
- **Track record:** none in Parliament. Its best result was 2.44% in 2017 ([MINOR_PARTIES.md](parties/MINOR_PARTIES.md)).

### 2.7 Te Pāti Māori (left-wing) – co-leaders Debbie Ngarewa-Packer and Rawiri Waititi

- **Stands for:** Māori self-determination grounded in Te Tiriti o Waitangi ([README](parties/te-pati-maori/README.md#1-summary)).
- **Strategy:** in 2026 it is asking Māori-roll voters for their electorate vote and telling supporters to give their party vote to
  Labour or the Greens ("one plan, two votes") ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1011909/te-pati-maori-reveals-election-strategy-as-campaign-launches-in-gisborne)).
- **Headline 2026 policies** ([91 policies](parties/te-pati-maori/policies/README.md)):
  - the "Kiwi Tax Plan": first $30,000 of income tax-free, a 48% rate over $300,000, a wealth tax, and a 33% company rate;
  - GST off kai (food);
  - an independent Te Tiriti Commission and binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations;
  - a Matike Mai constitution;
  - abolish prisons by 2040;
  - a $1b fund for Māori and community renewable energy.

  Source for the tax plan: [Kiwi Tax Plan PDF](https://img.scoop.co.nz/media/pdfs/2608/A_Kiwi_Tax_Plan.pdf).
- **Costings:** no overall costing found (same PDF).
- **Coalition:** the left bloc only. Its MPs fell from six to four over the term after two expulsions; the High Court found one of
  them unlawful ([README §6](parties/te-pati-maori/README.md#6-the-202526-internal-crisis)).
- **Track record:** delivery index 63% overall and 78% as National's support partner in 2008–17 (Whānau Ora, the UNDRIP endorsement,
  the Māori Language Act). Since 2020 it has been in opposition, and its track record rates its handling of its own internal process
  as "poor" ([track-record.md](parties/te-pati-maori/track-record.md#4-did-it-stick-to-its-word)).

## 4. Reliability and promise-keeping

### 4.1 Method: one standard for every party

The archive tracks **329 promises across eight parties** in [data/promises/](data/promises/). Each one has a verdict: *kept*,
*partially kept*, *broken*, *abandoned*, *in progress* or *not yet due*. Every entry carries sources and a `detail` field explaining
the verdict. This report recomputes every party's figures from those files using the same rules:

1. **Only resolved promises are scored.** Resolved means kept + partly kept + broken + abandoned. In-progress items (mostly from the
   current term) and 2026 pledges are left out of every percentage.
2. **Delivery index = (kept + ½ × partly kept) ÷ resolved.** This is the formula the ACT and NZ First pages already used
   ([ACT](parties/act/track-record.md#reliability-scorecard)); here it is applied to everyone. The kept % and the kept-or-partly % are
   shown alongside it.
3. **Role matters.** Each promise is assigned to the term it was meant for. That term is classed as *in office* (leading or in
   coalition), *support partner* (confidence and supply, or a cooperation agreement), or *opposition / out of Parliament*.
   - A party cannot deliver from opposition. Promises from lost campaigns are therefore nearly all "abandoned": their only test is
     whether the party kept advocating them.
   - The fairest comparison of reliability is the **in-office and support-partner columns** of the second table.

### 4.2 Caveats: read before comparing the numbers

- **Different sample sizes.** National (82 entries) and Labour (92) have far more tracked promises than Te Pāti Māori (21), the
  Greens (32) or Mana (4). United Future's 95% rests on ten negotiated items and nothing else. Small samples swing on one or two
  verdicts.
- **Selection.** Each file tracks the high-profile, checkable promises: pledge cards, flagship policies, 100-day plans and coalition
  agreements. None covers every manifesto line. The National file notes that adding the many small, low-profile promises would raise
  "kept" shares ([National caveats](parties/national/track-record.md#how-to-read-the-verdicts)). Labour's file says counts "would shift
  somewhat with a different selection" ([Labour method](parties/labour/track-record.md#10-method-and-caveats)).
- **Easy and hard promises.** Promises to repeal, legislate or pay out can almost always be delivered by a government with a majority.
  Promises about outcomes, such as surpluses, waiting times, homes built or child poverty, depend on the economy and on delivery
  capacity. Both major-party files find the same split:
  - Labour kept about 71% of its law and transfer promises outright, but only 2 of 13 build or outcome targets
    ([Labour §6](parties/labour/track-record.md#by-type-of-promise)).
  - About half of National's 2023–26 "kept" verdicts are repeals, while its misses are mostly outcomes
    ([National summary](parties/national/track-record.md#summary)).
  - So a government that mostly promises repeals will tend to score higher.
- **Government vs opposition vs support role.** Support partners such as the Greens, ACT 2008–17, the Māori Party and United Future
  promise less, and they bargain for specific items that can be written into an agreement. Their high rates partly reflect that.
- **Coalition constraints.**
  - Under MMP every government since 1996 has needed partners ([trends](elections/trends.md)).
  - NZ First blocked or diluted at least six Labour policies in 2017–20, including the CGT, the three-strikes repeal and light rail
    ([NZ First alignment](parties/nz-first/track-record.md#alignment-actions-vs-stated-policies-and-the-kingmaker-role)).
  - National lost its foreign-buyer tax and its super-age change to NZ First in 2023
    ([National README](parties/national/README.md#periods-in-government-and-arrangements)).
  - The National and Labour files mark promises lost in coalition talks as *abandoned*, not *broken*, and name the partner involved.
- **The files define "broken" slightly differently.**
  - National and Labour count a promise as broken only if it was missed "while in a position to deliver".
  - The ACT, NZ First, Green and Te Pāti Māori files count any non-delivery as broken, "whatever the reason", and explain the reason in
    `detail` ([Green how-to-read](parties/green/track-record.md#how-to-read-this)).
  - The effect is to make the smaller parties' broken counts slightly harsher. The kept and delivery-index figures are not affected.
- **External shocks.** Several records were hit by events outside the government's control:
  - the 2008–09 global financial crisis and the Canterbury earthquakes (Key);
  - COVID-19, then 7.3% inflation in 2022 (Ardern and Hipkins)
    ([Labour §3](parties/labour/track-record.md#3-covid-19-response));
  - the 2024 recession and the 2026 Middle East oil shock (Luxon) ([National caveats](parties/national/track-record.md#how-to-read-the-verdicts)).
- **Durability is a separate question.** At least 15 promises Labour kept were reversed by the 2023–26 coalition
  ([Labour durability](parties/labour/track-record.md#durability-what-survived-the-change-of-government)). ACT's charter schools and
  three strikes had been reversed by Labour in the past ([ACT trends](parties/act/track-record.md#trends-2011--2026)). A reversal does
  not change a "kept" verdict.
- **Other trackers differ.** The volunteer NZ Politics Promise Tracker lists 45 National promises: 23 kept, 18 in progress and 1
  broken. This archive finds more broken and partial verdicts, because it scores outcome promises
  ([National summary](parties/national/track-record.md#summary); [tracker](https://www.nzpoliticspromisetracker.nz/parties)).

**What the numbers do and don't show.** Measured in office or as a support partner, the six current parliamentary parties' delivery
indices fall in a fairly narrow band, about 59–78%. United Future, on ten items, is higher. That gap is small compared with the
uncertainty from selection and sample size. The clearer differences are in *what kind* of promise each party misses, set out below.

### 4.3 Where actions diverged from stated values: U-turns by party

Every party has some. The lists below are summaries of the "alignment" and "U-turn" sections of each track record, which give a
source for every item.

**National** ([full table](parties/national/track-record.md#notable-u-turns-and-changed-positions))
- GST: "not going to be raising GST" (2008), then raised it to 15% (2010)
  ([ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/politics/key-ruled-out-gst-increase-2008)).
- Fees-free: promised to scrap it (2019–20), then to keep it (2023), then moved it to the final year in coalition, then abolished it
  in Budget 2026.
- KiwiSaver: halved the government contribution (2025), said it would "remain voluntary" (Nov 2025), then promised **compulsory**
  KiwiSaver (2026).
- Super age: Key said it would never rise; English proposed 67 (2017); National proposed 67 again (2023); dropped in coalition.
- Fiscal prudence versus outcomes: promised a surplus in 2026/27; it is now forecast for 2028/29, on a new OBEGALx measure. Net debt
  is forecast to peak at 43.9% of GDP, above National's own 40% ceiling
  ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1647005/treasury-gives-willis-pre-election-boost-as-surplus-forecast-improves)).
- Major changes passed under urgency that had not been announced in National's 2023 campaign: the smokefree repeal and the Equal Pay
  Amendment Act 2025, which cancelled 33 pay-equity claims ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Amendment_Act_2025)).

**Labour** ([full list](parties/labour/track-record.md#notable-u-turns))
- Capital gains tax:
  - promised in 2011 and 2014, then dropped (2015);
  - ruled out in 2019 and in 2023 ("end of story"), against its own working group's or minister's advice;
  - promised again in 2025 ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/07/12/end-of-story-hipkins-rules-out-wealth-and-capital-gains-taxes)).
- Bright-line test: ruled out an extension in the 2020 campaign, then extended it five months later
  ([Newshub](https://newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/03/finance-minister-grant-robertson-admits-being-too-definitive-in-ruling-out-bright-line-extension-during-election.html)).
- KiwiBuild: the 100,000-home target was scrapped in 2019 ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/04-09-2019/cheat-sheet-megan-woods-hits-reset-on-the-beleaguered-kiwibuild-programme/)).
- Three Waters: presented as optional, then made mandatory (2021).
- The 2023 "policy bonfire" of its own programme ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/24-04-2023/purged-punted-and-pruned-the-chris-hipkins-reprioritisation-in-full)).
- Interest deductibility: removed it, then opposed its restoration, then ruled out changing it again (Sept 2026)
  ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/09/21/labour-rules-out-interest-deductibility-changes-for-landlords/)).

**Green** ([actions vs values](parties/green/track-record.md#5-actions-vs-values))
- Waka-jumping: voted for the waka-jumping law (2018) under the support agreement, voted to repeal it (2020–21), then used it to expel
  Darleen Tana (2024).
- Green School: an $11.7m grant to a private school (2020), against the party's policy. The party admitted the breach and the grant
  became a loan.
- Conduct of individual MPs: the Ghahraman convictions; the Tana and Genter findings.
- Wealth tax: the 2020 wealth tax and the 2023 Guaranteed Minimum Income were scaled back; the wealth-tax threshold rose from $2m to
  $10m for 2026.

**ACT** ([alignment](parties/act/track-record.md#alignment-did-acts-actions-match-its-stated-principles))
- Treaty referendum: described as a coalition "condition" in 2022, then dropped in 2023.
- Free expression: voted for the gang-patch ban despite its free-expression principles.
- Law-making process: champions careful law-making through the Regulatory Standards Act, yet the pay-equity changes, led by its own
  minister, passed under urgency without a select-committee stage.
- Public service: the promise to return it to its 2017 size was missed. FTEs in June 2026 (63,912) were about where they were in 2023.
- Immigration: moved from liberalising (2023) to restrictive (2026).

**NZ First** ([alignment](parties/nz-first/track-record.md#alignment-actions-vs-stated-policies-and-the-kingmaker-role))
- Regulatory Standards Act: voted it through all its stages (Nov 2025), then pledged a week later to repeal it.
- Oil and gas: part of the government that banned offshore exploration in 2018, then repealed the ban in 2025.
- Public Service Act: helped pass its diversity provisions in 2020, then moved to remove them in 2025.
- Fees-free: won its move to the final year, then agreed to scrap it.
- Historic: campaigned against National in 1996 and then went into government with it.

**Te Pāti Māori** ([actions vs kaupapa](parties/te-pati-maori/track-record.md#5-actions-vs-kaupapa))
- Foreshore and seabed: accepted the 2011 compromise that replaced the 2004 Act, which its own founder criticised.
- General seats: announced it would stand in general seats (April 2025), then stood only in Māori seats.
- Internal process: the High Court found its expulsion of Kapa-Kingi unlawful.
- Donations: disclosed 2020 donations late, a breach of electoral-finance rules. No prosecution followed.

**United Future and Mana** (historical): United Future's two signature policies, income splitting and "flexi-super", got only
procedural wins ([UF](parties/united-future/track-record.md#assessment)). Mana's Internet Party alliance raised its party vote but cost
Harawira his seat ([Mana](parties/mana/track-record.md#assessment)).

- **Fragmentation is rising.** In 2023 National and Labour together won only 65% of the vote, the lowest since 2002, and the effective
  number of parties reached its highest level in this series (table above). October 2026 polls put the two together at about 57%
  (§1).
- **The wasted vote** peaked at 7.8% in 2020 ([trends §3](elections/trends.md#3-turnout-overhang-and-the-wasted-vote)).
  - In 2026 it hinges on TOP: about 2% if TOP clears 5%, about 7% if it does not (scenario D, §1).
  - The 2012 MMP review's recommendation to lower the threshold to 4% was never legislated (same source).
- **Turnout:**
  - It ranged from 74.2% (2011) to 82.2% (2020).
  - Enrolment now closes 13 days before polling day, and prisoners are barred from voting under the Electoral Amendment Act 2025
    ([elections/2026.md](elections/2026.md#rule-changes-since-2023)).
  - By 15 October 2026, 65.5% of 18–24-year-olds were enrolled (same source).
- **Overhang:**
  - The 2023 House had 123 seats, the most under MMP (§6.4).
  - The 2026 House starts at 120 seats: 71 electorates and 49 list seats, with one more list seat than in 2023
    ([data/elections/2026.json](data/elections/2026.json)).

### 6.5 Minor-party cycles

- **NZ First** rises and falls. It was out in 2008, back in 2011, kingmaker in 2017, out in 2020 and in coalition in 2023. Each time
  it has left a coalition its support has collapsed ([NZ First trends](parties/nz-first/track-record.md#trends-2011--2026)).
- **ACT** survived on Epsom alone at 0.5–1.1% (2011–17), then won 7.6–8.6% (2020–23) ([trends §5–6](elections/trends.md#6-electorate-deals-coat-tailing-epsom-and-ōhāriu)).
- **The Greens** are the most stable minor party (6–12%). They do better in opposition than in government
  ([Green trends](parties/green/track-record.md#6-trends)).
- **Small parties near the threshold:** the Conservatives' 3.97% in 2014 was the biggest near-miss. COVID-era protest parties won
  about 1–2% combined in 2020 and 2023. TOP polled above 5% for the first time in 2026, peaking at 9.5% (Roy Morgan, August)
  ([MINOR_PARTIES.md](parties/MINOR_PARTIES.md); [TOP README](parties/opportunity/README.md#2026-campaign-summary)).

## 8. Data quality and limitations

**Blocked or unreachable sources, and the workarounds used:**

- **Party websites:** greens.org.nz, nzfirst.nz, maoriparty.org.nz and opportunity.org.nz block automated access (Cloudflare 403,
  including from a headless browser), and web.archive.org could not be reached ([docs/AGENT_BRIEF.md](docs/AGENT_BRIEF.md)).
  - Their web pages were recovered from **Common Crawl** captures, dated July–October 2026. These may predate later edits.
  - Press releases were taken from the party's own releases mirrored on **Scoop**, and PDFs from the parties' file hosts.
  - Each method is described in the party's policies README, for example the [Green](parties/green/policies/README.md),
    [NZ First](parties/nz-first/policies/README.md) and [TOP](parties/opportunity/policies/README.md) policy pages.
- **Pages that could not be recovered:**
  - Seven nzfirst.nz pages, one maoriparty.org.nz page and three opportunity.org.nz pages. Each has a `not-retrieved` placeholder that
    gives the URL and the reason, with no paraphrase.
  - Green: the disability policy PDF and the 23 Oct fiscal plan itself (reported via RNZ).
  - nzloyal.com ([NZ Loyal note](parties/nz-loyal/policies/documents/nzloyal-com-not-retrievable.md)).
- **Official results:** electionresults.govt.nz was blocked. Results come from Wikipedia's tables, which cite the official counts, and
  2023 electorate majorities were cross-checked against each electorate's article ([trends sources](elections/trends.md#sources);
  [electorates/README.md](electorates/README.md#about-the-data)).
- **Parliament and legislation:** parliament.nz and legislation.govt.nz could not be fetched. Bill dates come from news reports and
  Wikipedia ([NZ First policies](parties/nz-first/policies/README.md)).
- **Coalition agreements:** the 2023 coalition-agreement PDFs returned 403, so their contents come from reporting
  ([NZ First track record](parties/nz-first/track-record.md#how-to-read-this)).
- **Old manifestos:** Labour's 2017 and 2020 manifesto PDFs could not be obtained, so the wording of those promises comes from
  contemporary news and official releases ([Labour method](parties/labour/track-record.md#10-method-and-caveats)).
- **Other trackers:** the Parliament Pulse tracker's data could not be read ([National gaps](parties/national/track-record.md#gaps-and-things-this-archive-could-not-verify)).

**Second-hand sources:**

- The poll series is Wikipedia's table, with each row linked to the pollster's own release
  ([data/polls-2026.json](data/polls-2026.json)).
- Party summaries in [elections/2026.md](elections/2026.md) come from campaign coverage collated on Wikipedia.
- Policy "Why/How" summaries are policy.nz's (`summary_source` in each `policies.json`). The verbatim party texts sit beside them in
  `documents/`.
- The **official candidate count** was not retrievable. policy.nz lists 470 electorate candidacies, which should be treated as
  approximate ([elections/2026.md](elections/2026.md#who-is-standing)).

| Te Pāti Māori "bottom line" | NZ First's leader said Te Pāti Māori called its tax policy a "bottom line"; no Te Pāti Māori statement using that phrase was found | [TPM policies](parties/te-pati-maori/policies/README.md) |

**How to verify anything in this report:**

1. Follow the link on the sentence. For archive files, follow the source links inside them. Promise entries carry `sources` arrays.
2. For policy wording, open `parties/<party>/policies/documents/<doc>.md`, which holds the verbatim published text with its source URL
   and retrieval date in the front matter.
3. For numbers, run `python3 tools/report_stats.py`, and see [docs/SCHEMA.md](docs/SCHEMA.md) for the data formats.
4. For official results, enrolment and voting places, the primary source is the Electoral Commission:
   [vote.nz](https://vote.nz) and [elections.nz](https://elections.nz).
5. Snapshot date: everything is as of 23 October 2026. Parties were still releasing policy, and new polls will follow
   ([quiz-method.md §4](guide/quiz-method.md#4-limitations)).

README.md:
# Ballot Book NZ — an independent guide to New Zealand politics, 2011–2026

A sourced, non-partisan research archive for voters in the **7 November 2026 general election**: every party, every 2026 policy (summary **and** full original text), every candidate and MP since 2011, how each party has kept its promises, and how Parliament has been made up at every election since 2011.

**Live site: https://not-simon.github.io/Politicsnz/**

It comes with an interactive, phone-friendly guide in [`site/`](site/), organised around five questions: **Today** (what to do now, what's new), **Vote** (am I enrolled, how and where do I vote, who's standing where I live), **Choose** (policy swipe, find-your-match quiz, values compass, a two-player game, compare two parties), **Parties** (every party, policy, issue, person, promise and press release) and **Seats** (polls and forecast, the electorate map since 2011, Parliament, coalition builder, seat calculator, election-night results). Design notes are in [`site/redesign/`](site/redesign/IA.md).

> Not affiliated with any party. Every fact is meant to link to its source, and the same rules apply to every party ([editorial standards](docs/EDITORIAL_STANDARDS.md)). If you find an error, open a [Correction issue](https://github.com/not-simon/Politicsnz/issues/new/choose) or see [how to report an error](docs/EDITORIAL_STANDARDS.md#how-to-report-an-error). Party policy texts are reproduced as published, for reference. Enrol and find your voting place at **vote.nz**.

## Start here

| If you want… | Go to |
|---|---|
| The big picture: who's offering what, who keeps promises, trends | [`REPORT.md`](REPORT.md) |
| Plain-English party summaries | [`guide/parties.md`](guide/parties.md) |
| Where every party stands on the big issues | [`guide/issues.md`](guide/issues.md) |
| Your electorate and its candidates | [`electorates/`](electorates/README.md) |
| Every 2026 policy of one party, with full texts | `parties/<party>/policies/README.md` (e.g. [National](parties/national/policies/README.md), [Labour](parties/labour/policies/README.md), [Green](parties/green/policies/README.md), [ACT](parties/act/policies/README.md), [NZ First](parties/nz-first/policies/README.md), [Te Pāti Māori](parties/te-pati-maori/policies/README.md), [TOP](parties/opportunity/policies/README.md)) |
| Has a party kept its word? | `parties/<party>/track-record.md` and [`data/promises/`](data/promises/) |
| A politician's profile | `parties/<party>/people/<name>/README.md` (each has `photo.jpg` and `person.json`) |
| Each election 2011–2023 and what's ahead in 2026 | [`elections/`](elections/) and [`elections/trends.md`](elections/trends.md) |
| Minor parties, past and present | [`parties/MINOR_PARTIES.md`](parties/MINOR_PARTIES.md) |
| How the quiz works | [`guide/quiz-method.md`](guide/quiz-method.md) |

## What's in it

- **1,435 policies** from 20 parties and groups standing in 2026, backed by **993 full-text documents** (party web pages, policy PDFs, press releases) in `parties/<party>/policies/documents/`. Each policy has a summary (Why / How), its topic and links to the verbatim source.

  | Party | Policies | | Party | Policies |
  |---|---:|---|---|---:|
  | Green | 564 | | Animal Justice | 38 |
  | National | 159 | | Vision NZ | 35 |
  | Labour | 126 | | Alliance | 27 |
  | ACT | 110 | | Te Tai Tokerau Party | 22 |
  | Te Pāti Māori | 91 | | Conservative | 19 |
  | NZ First | 79 | | Outdoors & Freedom | 18 |
  | TOP (Opportunity) | 77 | | Women's Rights, Legalise Cannabis, NZ Loyal, Free Palestine + electorate-only groups | 70 |

  The Greens' count is high because their whole manifesto and 40 standing policy papers are itemised.
- **People:** profile folders for MPs who served 2011–2026 and every 2026 candidate (≈550 people, most with photos), with current status (MP, retiring, candidate, former MP and what they do now).
- **Track records:** promise-by-promise checks for National, Labour, Green, ACT, NZ First and Te Pāti Māori (plus United Future and Mana), with verdicts *kept / partly kept / broken / abandoned / in progress* and sources.
- **Elections:** full results 2008–2023 (every party, every electorate, official counts), membership of the 50th–54th Parliaments including every mid-term change, and 129 opinion polls since 2023.
- **2026 guide layer:** plain-English cards for all 17 registered parties, 17 issue explainers with key facts, a 45-question match quiz with sourced party positions, and guides to all 71 electorates.

## Folder layout

```
REPORT.md                 the comprehensive report
guide/                    plain-English party cards, issues, quiz method
elections/                one story per election + trends
electorates/              one page per 2026 electorate
parties/<party>/
  README.md               profile: history, leaders, results, 2026 pitch, coalition stance
  track-record.md         promises vs delivery
  policies/               README (every policy) · policies.json · documents/ (full texts)
  people/<person>/        README.md · person.json · photo.jpg
data/                     machine-readable JSON (elections, parliaments, polls, promises, guide, electorates)
raw/                      source downloads (policy.nz data, policy PDFs)
site/                     the interactive guide (open site/index.html via any static web server)
tools/                    the scripts that fetched and built everything
docs/SCHEMA.md            data formats
```

## Viewing the interactive guide

- **Locally:** `cd site && python3 -m http.server` then open http://localhost:8000.
- **GitHub Pages:** the workflow in `.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes `site/` automatically. Turn it on under *Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions*. (Pages on a private repository needs a paid GitHub plan; on a public repository it's free.)
- **Rebuild after editing data:** `python3 tools/build_site.py`.

## Editorial standards and corrections

- The rules the guide is written to (neutral wording, equal treatment of every party, sourced and dated facts, attributed
  criticism, plain English) are in [`docs/EDITORIAL_STANDARDS.md`](docs/EDITORIAL_STANDARDS.md).
- Every change made in the pre-publication fact-check and neutrality review, with before/after wording and the reason, is in
  [`docs/REVIEW_LOG.md`](docs/REVIEW_LOG.md). It also lists issues found outside the reviewed files that still need follow-up.
- To report an error: open an issue with the **Correction** template (say which page, what is wrong, what is right, and link a
  source), or email the maintainer. Corrections are checked against the party's own published text or the official source.

## Licence, privacy and contact

- Code is MIT; the project's own text and data are CC BY-SA 4.0 (parts are adapted from Wikipedia, which requires that); third-party material stays its owners' and is listed in [`NOTICE.md`](NOTICE.md). Owners can ask for removal or correction by [opening an issue](https://github.com/not-simon/Politicsnz/issues/new/choose); we act within 24 hours during the campaign.
- Published by an unincorporated group of volunteers led by the repository owner. Not affiliated with any party, candidate or the Electoral Commission. Official voting information is at vote.nz.
- The site has no accounts, cookies, server or analytics; answers are kept in the visitor's own browser. See the privacy statement on the site's *Why trust this?* page and the compliance notes in [`docs/LEGAL_REVIEW.md`](docs/LEGAL_REVIEW.md).
- On election night a workflow reads the Electoral Commission's public results feed every five minutes from 7pm and the Seats › Results page refreshes itself; preliminary figures are labelled, and the official result (27 November) replaces them.
- Automated updates (polls, releases) are paused from 23:59 Friday 6 November to 7pm Saturday 7 November (NZDT); on election day the site hides polls, forecasts, quiz results and the game until 7pm (Electoral Act 1993 s 197).

## Sources and method

Sources include party websites and policy documents, policy.nz (structured 2026 policy and candidate data), the Electoral Commission, Parliament, the Beehive, Wikipedia (for election tables and biographies, with the primary sources it cites), and news media (RNZ, Stuff, NZ Herald, The Spinoff, interest.co.nz, 1News). Some party sites (Green, NZ First, Te Pāti Māori, TOP, NZ Loyal) block automated access; their texts came from Common Crawl archive captures, the parties' own releases on Scoop, and party PDFs — each document records how and when it was captured. Gaps and source disagreements are listed in each README rather than papered over. Retrieved 23 October 2026; policies may change before election day.

# 2011 New Zealand general election (26 November 2011)

> Part of the [elections archive](trends.md). Structured data: [`data/elections/2011.json`](../data/elections/2011.json) ·
> Parliament it produced: [`data/parliaments/50.json`](../data/parliaments/50.json). Tables between `GENERATED` markers are built
> by `tools/elections_md.py` from the JSON; the narrative is hand-written from the sources listed at the end.

## At a glance

- **Winner:** National (John Key) – 47.31% of the party vote and 59 of 121 seats, the best National result under MMP up to that point,
  but two seats short of a majority on its own.
- **Government:** a second-term **National minority government** with confidence-and-supply agreements with ACT (1 seat),
  United Future (1) and the Māori Party (3) – 64 of 121 seats. New ministry appointed 14 December 2011.
- **Opposition:** Labour (Phil Goff) fell to 27.48% and 34 seats; Goff resigned and David Shearer became leader in December 2011.
- **Big movers:** the Greens reached 11.06% (14 seats), their best result to that date; NZ First returned to Parliament with 6.59%
  (8 seats) after missing out in 2008; ACT collapsed to 1.07% and survived only through John Banks winning Epsom.
- **Referendum:** held alongside the election, 57.8% voted to **keep MMP**.
- **Turnout:** 74.21% of enrolled electors, which Wikipedia describes as the lowest turnout since 1887.

## Context

National had governed since November 2008 as a minority government (58 of 122 seats) supported by ACT, United Future and the Māori
Party. The 49th Parliament covered the aftermath of the global financial crisis and the Canterbury earthquakes of 2010–11, and the
election date was fixed – unusually early, in February 2011 – for 26 November, after New Zealand hosted the Rugby World Cup
(9 September – 23 October 2011), which ruled out dates in that window.

Key's decision to announce the date early broke with the tradition of keeping it secret as long as possible. The writ return was
later delayed from 15 to 17 December because the judicial recount in Waitakere was not finished in time.

## Campaign and issues

- **Partial asset sales ("mixed ownership").** National campaigned on selling minority stakes in state-owned energy companies and
  reducing the Crown's share of Air New Zealand. After the election Key rejected claims the government lacked a mandate for the
  policy. Opponents later forced the 2013 citizens-initiated referendum on the sales (held by postal ballot, Nov–Dec 2013), which the
  government said it would ignore because the 2011 election had given it a mandate.
- **Capital gains tax.** Labour went into 2011 (and again 2014) with a capital gains tax policy – a point noted in the 2017 election
  article when Labour finally dropped the idea for its first term. Phil Goff's Wikipedia biography records an earlier leaked capital
  gains tax proposal that critics saw as unpopular.
- **The Epsom "tea tape".** On 11 November Key met ACT's Epsom candidate John Banks for a cup of tea in a Newmarket café to signal to
  Epsom voters that they should give their electorate vote to ACT and their party vote to National – a deal that lets a small party
  bypass the 5% threshold by winning one electorate. A recording of the conversation, made by a device left on the table, was passed
  to the *Herald on Sunday* and dominated the last fortnight of the campaign. Banks won Epsom by 2,261 votes over National's Paul
  Goldsmith.
- **Coalition signals.** National ruled out working with Winston Peters; ACT committed to National; Goff ruled out a coalition with
  Hone Harawira's new Mana Party but left the door open to NZ First; the Greens preferred Labour but did not rule out National;
  United Future ruled out Labour; the Māori Party would not work in government with ACT.
- **Media coverage.** A Massey University study (released Nov 2012) found the four big newspapers printed 72% more photos of Key than
  of Goff in the last month and gave him twice as many column inches.

Main party pitches in one line each (a summary; detailed 2011 manifesto texts were not re-checked against primary sources for this archive): **National** – economic management,
returning to surplus and the mixed-ownership programme; **Labour** – opposing asset sales and a capital gains tax excluding the
family home; **Greens** – jobs, child poverty and clean rivers; **NZ First** – opposing asset sales and protecting superannuation;
**ACT** (under Don Brash) – smaller government; **Mana** – a new kaupapa Māori/left party formed by Hone Harawira after he left the
Māori Party.

## Results

**Government formed:** Fifth National Government (second term) – PM John Key – National (minority government with confidence & supply); support: ACT (confidence & supply), United Future (confidence & supply), Te Pāti Māori / Māori Party (confidence & supply); sworn in 2011-12-14.

National (59 seats) renewed confidence-and-supply agreements with ACT (1), United Future (1) and the Māori Party (3): 64 of 121 seats. New ministry appointed at Government House 14 Dec 2011. The election was held alongside a referendum on retaining MMP (MMP retained, 57.8%).
<!-- GENERATED:results END -->

### What the numbers meant

- **National's high-water mark.** National's 47.31% was close to a majority of votes cast for parties that won seats, but the
  Sainte-Laguë allocation still left it at 59 seats – two short of 61 in a 121-seat House – so it again depended on small partners.
- **The support parties shrank.** ACT went from 5 seats to 1, the Māori Party from 5 to 3 (losing Te Tai Tonga to Labour's Rino
  Tirikatene), and United Future held only Peter Dunne's Ōhāriu seat. Together they still gave the government 64 votes.
- **Overhang.** The Māori Party's three electorates exceeded its party-vote entitlement, creating one overhang seat (121 MPs).
- **Wasted vote.** 3.37% of valid party votes went to parties that won no seats – the lowest of the six elections in this archive,
  mainly because the Conservatives (2.65%) were the only sizeable party left out.
- **Labour's low.** 27.48% was Labour's worst result in decades at the time (it fell further in 2014). Goff and deputy Annette King
  resigned on 29 November; David Shearer beat David Cunliffe for the leadership.
- **ACT leadership.** Don Brash resigned as ACT leader on election night, taking responsibility for the result.

## Electorates

70 electorates (63 general, 7 Māori). Notable contests:

- **Waitakere** – National's Paula Bennett held on by just 9 votes over Labour's Carmel Sepuloni after a judicial recount (the delay
  pushed back the return of the writ).
- **Christchurch Central** – National's Nicky Wagner took the seat from Labour's Brendon Burns by 47 votes – the first time National
  had won the seat; part of a Canterbury swing in a year dominated by the earthquake recovery.
- **Epsom** – ACT's John Banks won with National's tacit support (see above).
- **Te Tai Tokerau** – Hone Harawira kept the seat for his new Mana Party (majority 1,165 over Labour's Kelvin Davis), having won it
  at a June 2011 by-election after leaving the Māori Party.
- **West Coast-Tasman** – Labour's Damien O'Connor regained the seat from National.
- **Wigram** – Labour's Megan Woods succeeded the retiring Jim Anderton (Progressive), ending the Progressive Party's presence in
  Parliament.

## Government formation

National renewed its confidence-and-supply arrangements with ACT, United Future and the Māori Party in December 2011. Governor-General Sir Jerry Mateparae appointed the new ministry on 14 December 2011, with 24 National ministers and four
ministers from support parties. The arrangement – a large party governing in minority with one-seat partners – was the high point of
"electorate-deal" politics in New Zealand: ACT and United Future were in Parliament only because they won Epsom and Ōhāriu.

## The 50th Parliament (2011–2014)

Notable changes: NZ First expelled list MP Brendan Horan from its caucus in December 2012 (he sat as an independent and later
founded the NZ Independent Coalition); United Future was briefly deregistered in mid-2013, leaving Peter Dunne technically an
independent; by-elections in Ikaroa-Rāwhiti (Meka Whaitiri, Labour, June 2013) and Christchurch East (Poto Williams, Labour,
November 2013); and ACT's John Banks resigned in June 2014 after being convicted of filing a false electoral return (the conviction was
later overturned), leaving ACT without an MP until the election.

## What changed

1. MMP was confirmed by referendum, triggering the Electoral Commission's 2012 MMP review (which recommended a 4% threshold and
   abolishing the one-electorate "coat-tail" rule – recommendations Parliament did not adopt; see [2014](2014.md)).
2. The Greens established themselves as the clear third party (11%), and NZ First showed it could come back from outside Parliament.
3. The election entrenched the pattern of National relying on small electorate-based partners, and of Labour struggling with
   leadership changes (Goff → Shearer → Cunliffe → Little before 2017).

# 2014 New Zealand general election (20 September 2014)

> Structured data: [`data/elections/2014.json`](../data/elections/2014.json) · Parliament: [`data/parliaments/51.json`](../data/parliaments/51.json).
> Tables between `GENERATED` markers are rebuilt by `tools/elections_md.py`.

## At a glance

- **Winner:** National (John Key) – 47.04% and 60 of 121 seats. On election night National had 61 seats, an outright majority, but it
  lost one seat to the Greens when special votes were counted (official results 4 October 2014).
- **Government:** third-term **National minority government**, again with confidence-and-supply partners ACT (1), United Future (1)
  and the Māori Party (2). Ministry sworn in 8 October 2014.
- **Labour** (David Cunliffe) fell to 25.13% and 32 seats – its lowest party-vote share of the MMP era. Cunliffe resigned and Andrew
  Little became leader in November 2014.
- **NZ First** rose to 8.66% (11 seats); the **Greens** were steady at 10.70% (14).
- **Missed out:** the Conservatives (3.97%) and Internet MANA (1.42%) – together more than 129,000 party votes with no seats. Hone
  Harawira lost Te Tai Tokerau, ending Mana's parliamentary presence.
- **Turnout:** 77.90%, with a record 717,579 advance votes (more than double 2011).

## Context

The 50th Parliament had been turbulent for National's support partners: ACT's only MP John Banks resigned in June 2014 after being
convicted (later overturned) of filing a false electoral return; United Future was deregistered for some weeks in 2013; and NZ First
expelled Brendan Horan. The Electoral Commission's 2012 MMP review had recommended lowering the party-vote threshold from 5% to 4% and
abolishing the "one electorate seat" coat-tail rule, but in May 2014 the government announced there was no cross-party consensus and it
would not legislate. So 2014 was fought under the same rules – and the same Epsom/Ōhāriu arrangements – as 2011.

The government had carried out its partial asset sales (Mighty River Power, Meridian and Genesis floated, Crown share cut from 100% to
51%), despite a 2013 citizens-initiated referendum in which a majority opposed them.

## Campaign and issues

- **Dirty Politics.** On 13 August Nicky Hager published *Dirty Politics*, based on hacked emails of blogger Cameron Slater, alleging
  that National Party figures and ministerial staff fed "attack politics" through right-wing blogs. It led to Justice Minister Judith
  Collins resigning as a minister on 30 August after an email suggested she had tried to undermine the head of the Serious Fraud Office.
- **Kim Dotcom and the "Moment of Truth".** The Internet Party, funded by Kim Dotcom, ran a joint list with Hone Harawira's Mana
  Movement ("Internet MANA"), relying on Harawira holding Te Tai Tokerau to bring list MPs in on his coat-tails. On 15 September it
  held "The Moment of Truth" with Glenn Greenwald, Edward Snowden and Julian Assange, about New Zealand's role in Five Eyes surveillance.
  Late in the campaign National's John Key and NZ First's Winston Peters publicly endorsed Labour's Kelvin Davis in Te Tai Tokerau.
- **Housing.** National promised to let KiwiSaver members withdraw member tax credits for a first home, double the KiwiSaver first-home
  deposit subsidy and raise the house-price caps. Labour campaigned on KiwiBuild-style state building and a **capital gains tax**
  excluding the family home – Cunliffe stumbled in *The Press* debate when he could not say whether family homes held in trusts would
  be exempt.
- **Health.** Labour launched (10 August) with free GP visits and prescriptions for pregnant women, under-13s and over-65s.
- **ACT** (new leader Jamie Whyte) promised to repeal the Resource Management Act and abolish the Overseas Investment Office.
- **Electricity.** Labour and the Greens promised reform of the wholesale electricity market (a single buyer, "NZ Power") to cut power
  prices; the power company share prices jumped after National's win.
- **Coalition signals.** Key urged voters not to split the party vote ("If you want steak for dinner tonight, go and buy steak");
  Cunliffe said he would work with the Greens and NZ First; both leaders ruled out working with Internet MANA.

### Reading the result

- **The "wasted" vote** returned to 6.24% of valid party votes – the Conservatives' 3.97% was the largest single vote ever to miss the
  threshold in this period, and it went entirely unrepresented.
- **Coat-tails both ways.** ACT (0.69%) and United Future (0.22%) won seats only through Epsom and Ōhāriu; Internet MANA (1.42%) won
  nothing because Harawira lost his electorate by 743 votes. United Future's seat was an **overhang** (it was entitled to none on the
  party vote), making the House 121.
- **Māori electorates.** Labour won six of seven – taking Tāmaki Makaurau and Te Tai Hauāuru from the Māori Party after Pita Sharples
  and Tariana Turia retired, and Te Tai Tokerau from Mana. The Māori Party kept only Waiariki (Te Ururoa Flavell) plus one list seat
  (Marama Fox).
- **Labour's split-vote problem.** Labour won 34.13% of electorate votes but only 25.13% of party votes – many voters backed Labour
  candidates locally but gave their party vote elsewhere (largely Greens and NZ First).

## Electorates

71 electorates (64 general, 7 Māori). Boundary changes created **Kelston** and **Upper Harbour** and abolished **Waitakere**. Notable:

- **Napier** – Labour's Stuart Nash won after National's retiring Chris Tremain's seat split between National's Wayne Walford and
  Conservative Garth McVicar.
- **Te Tai Tokerau** – Kelvin Davis (Labour) beat Hone Harawira (Internet MANA) by 743; Harawira's request for a judicial recount
  upheld the result.
- **Auckland Central** – Nikki Kaye (National) held off Jacinda Ardern by 600, the closest seat in the country.
- **Epsom** – ACT's new candidate David Seymour won by 4,250 over National's Paul Goldsmith, who again ran a party-vote-only campaign.

## Government formation

With 60 seats, National needed one more vote. It re-signed confidence-and-supply agreements with United Future (29 Sep 2014), ACT, and the
Māori Party (5 Oct 2014), giving it 64 votes in a 121-seat House, and the ministry was sworn in on 8 October 2014. John Key resigned as
Prime Minister in December 2016; Bill English succeeded him on 12 December 2016.

## The 51st Parliament (2014–2017)

The most consequential change was the **2015 Northland by-election** (28 March 2015): after National MP Mike Sabin resigned,
Winston Peters won the safe National seat for NZ First, cutting the government's working majority and showing the vulnerability of
provincial seats. Phil Goff (Mount Roskill) and David Shearer (Mount Albert) resigned and were replaced at by-elections by Michael
Wood and **Jacinda Ardern**; John Key and David Cunliffe resigned within six months of the 2017 election, so their seats were left vacant.

## What changed

1. Electorate deals proved fragile: the coat-tail rule saved ACT and United Future but failed Internet MANA.
2. The Conservatives' near-miss (3.97%) became the standard example of the 5% threshold's cost in "wasted" votes.
3. Labour's third successive defeat pushed it toward the leadership change (Little, then Ardern in 2017) that transformed 2017.
4. Labour reclaimed the Māori electorates (6 of 7), a dominance that lasted until 2023.

# 2017 New Zealand general election (23 September 2017)

> Structured data: [`data/elections/2017.json`](../data/elections/2017.json) · Parliament: [`data/parliaments/52.json`](../data/parliaments/52.json).
> Tables between `GENERATED` markers are rebuilt by `tools/elections_md.py`.

## At a glance

- **Largest party:** National (Bill English) – 44.45%, 56 of 120 seats, but no majority even with ACT (57).
- **Government:** **Labour–NZ First coalition** with **Green confidence and supply** (46 + 9 + 8 = 63 of 120). NZ First announced its
  choice on 19 October 2017; the government was sworn in on 26 October with **Jacinda Ardern** as Prime Minister and Winston Peters as
  Deputy PM. It was the first time under MMP that a party led a government without winning the most party votes.
- **Labour's surge:** 36.89% (+11.76 pp) and 46 seats after Ardern replaced Andrew Little as leader just seven weeks before polling day.
- **Fewest parties under MMP:** only five parties entered Parliament (National, Labour, NZ First, Greens, ACT). The Māori Party
  (1.18%) lost all its seats, and United Future did not return after Peter Dunne retired.
- **TOP** (Gareth Morgan's Opportunities Party, founded 2016) won 2.44% but no seats.
- **Turnout:** 79.75%.

## Context

National was seeking a fourth term – no government had won four terms since 1972 and none had under MMP. John Key resigned
unexpectedly in December 2016 and Bill English, his finance minister, became Prime Minister. Labour began 2017 polling in the
mid-20s under Andrew Little; on **1 August 2017** Little resigned and deputy leader Jacinda Ardern was elected unopposed, with Kelvin
Davis as deputy. Labour reported $250,000 in donations and 1,000 new volunteers within 24 hours.

The Greens had a turbulent campaign: co-leader **Metiria Turei** disclosed in July that she had not told Work and Income about
flatmates' rent while on a benefit in the 1990s, and later that she had enrolled at a false address in 1993. Two Green MPs (David
Clendon, Kennedy Graham) quit the caucus and Turei resigned as co-leader on 9 August, leaving James Shaw as sole leader.

## Campaign and issues

A Roy Morgan poll in January 2017 found 26% of respondents named housing supply and affordability the most important issue and 17%
poverty and inequality.

- **Housing.** House prices nationally rose 34.2% between June 2014 and June 2017 (45.5% in Auckland). Labour's flagship was
  **KiwiBuild** (100,000 homes in 10 years), plus extending the bright-line test from two to five years, ending negative gearing and
  tenancy changes (90-day notice, no termination without cause, rent rises at most yearly). The Greens wanted a **capital gains tax**
  (excluding the family home) in the first term; ACT wanted to scrap Auckland's urban growth boundary.
- **Tax.** Labour would reverse the 2017 Budget tax cuts and put the money into Working for Families and a new payment for families
  with children under three (the Best Start policy), plus a winter energy payment. Nine days before the election, finance spokesman
  Grant Robertson promised **"no new taxes or levies" until after the 2020 election** – any capital gains tax from a tax working group
  would not take effect until 2021.
- **Immigration.** Net migration was 72,300 in the year to June 2017. Labour promised to cut it by 20–30,000 a year (mainly by
  tightening "low-value" student visas); NZ First wanted it cut to about 10,000; National tightened skilled-migrant pay thresholds.
- **Education.** Labour promised three years' **fees-free tertiary education** (first year from 2018) and a $50/week rise in student
  allowances; National pledged a $379 million education package; ACT offered bulk-funding with large teacher pay rises.
- **Poverty.** At the 4 September debate English committed to lifting 100,000 children out of poverty; Ardern committed to legislating
  child-poverty measurement in every Budget.
- **Infrastructure/transport.** National promised ten new "Roads of National Significance" ($10.5 billion) and $267 million for
  Auckland and Wellington commuter rail; Labour promised Auckland light rail (CBD–airport within a decade) and Auckland–Hamilton–Tauranga
  rail; the Greens proposed Wellington light rail.
- **NZ First** campaigned on regional development, cutting immigration, keeping super at 65, moving the Ports of Auckland to Northport,
  and referendums on abolishing the Māori seats and reducing Parliament to 100 MPs.
- **Water and environment.** The Greens proposed a 10c/litre levy on bottled water and a $2/kg nitrate (fertiliser) charge on farmers.

### Reading the result

- **Preliminary vs final.** Election night gave National 58 seats, Labour 45, NZ First 9, Greens 7, ACT 1. Special votes moved one
  seat each from National to Labour and the Greens, making NZ First the decisive "kingmaker": National+NZ First = 65, or
  Labour+NZ First+Greens = 63.
- **No overhang** (120 seats) – the first 120-seat House since 2002, because neither United Future nor the Māori Party won an electorate.
- **Minor-party squeeze.** Combined National+Labour vote was 81.34%, the highest of the six elections in this archive. The Greens
  (6.27%) halved; TOP's 2.44% and the Māori Party's 1.18% were "wasted" – 4.68% of valid party votes in total.
- **Māori electorates.** Labour won all seven – Tāmati Coffey beat Māori Party co-leader Te Ururoa Flavell in Waiariki – the first
  clean sweep since 2002, leaving the Māori Party out of Parliament.

## Electorates

71 electorates (64 general, 7 Māori). Notable:

- **Christchurch Central** – Labour's Duncan Webb took the seat back from National's Nicky Wagner.
- **Hutt South** – National list MP Chris Bishop beat Labour's Trevor Mallard, the first time the seat had changed hands since 1996
  (helped by boundary changes moving Naenae out).
- **Ōhāriu** – after Peter Dunne retired, Labour's Greg O'Connor won (majority 1,051).
- **Northland** – National's Matt King won back the seat from Winston Peters, who had won it at the 2015 by-election.
- **Epsom** – David Seymour (ACT) held on with National's tacit support; ACT's 0.50% party vote gave it no extra seats.
- **Hamilton West** was described as the country's bellwether.

## Government formation

Both National and Labour negotiated with NZ First, whose board and caucus met on 16 October. On **19 October** Winston Peters announced
a coalition with Labour; the Greens agreed confidence and supply the same day. NZ First received four Cabinet posts (Peters as Deputy
PM and Foreign Minister, plus Ron Mark, Tracey Martin, Shane Jones) and one under-secretary (Fletcher Tabuteau); the Greens three
ministers outside Cabinet (James Shaw, Julie Anne Genter, Eugenie Sage) and one under-secretary (Jan Logie). English had ruled out a
formal arrangement with ACT. The Sixth Labour Government was sworn in on **26 October 2017**.

## The 52nd Parliament (2017–2020)

Bill English and Steven Joyce resigned in 2018 (replaced by Maureen Pugh and Nicola Willis); the **2018 Northcote by-election** was
held by National's Dan Bidois; **Jami-Lee Ross** left National in October 2018 after a public dispute with leader Simon Bridges and sat
as an independent (later co-leading Advance NZ); National's Andrew Falloon resigned in July 2020, too close to the election for a
by-election. Notable legislation included the Zero Carbon Act, the End of Life Choice Act (put to a binding referendum in 2020), the
cannabis referendum commitment (from the Green agreement) and the post-Christchurch-mosque-attacks firearms ban (2019). The election
originally set for 19 September 2020 was delayed to 17 October because of COVID-19.

## What changed

1. The "largest party forms government" convention was broken – under MMP the bloc that can command 61 votes governs.
2. Parliament consolidated to five parties; electorate-deal partners (United Future, the Māori Party) disappeared.
3. NZ First's kingmaker role (as in 1996 and 2005) peaked; in 2020 it lost all its seats.

# 2020 New Zealand general election (17 October 2020)

> Structured data: [`data/elections/2020.json`](../data/elections/2020.json) · Parliament: [`data/parliaments/53.json`](../data/parliaments/53.json).
> Tables between `GENERATED` markers are rebuilt by `tools/elections_md.py`.

## At a glance

- **Landslide:** Labour (Jacinda Ardern) won **50.01%** of the party vote and **65 of 120 seats** – the first single-party majority
  since MMP began in 1996, the first time Labour had won an absolute majority of the vote since 1946, the best popular-vote result for any main party since 1951 and the
  most seats any party had won since 1990.
- **National** (Judith Collins) fell to 25.58% and 33 seats, its second-worst result ever (only 2002 was worse).
- **ACT** jumped from 1 seat to **10** (7.59%); the **Greens** won 10 seats (7.86%) – the first minor party to increase its vote after a
  term supporting a government – and Chlöe Swarbrick won **Auckland Central**, the Greens' first electorate since 1999.
- **NZ First** (2.60%) lost every seat; **Te Pāti Māori** returned with Rawiri Waititi winning Waiariki (+1 list seat).
- **Government:** Labour governed alone but signed a **cooperation agreement** with the Greens (31 Oct 2020). Sworn in 6 Nov 2020.
- **Turnout:** 82.24% – the highest of the six elections in this archive.
- **Referendums:** the End of Life Choice Act was approved (65.1%); recreational cannabis legalisation was narrowly rejected (50.7% no).

## Context

The 2017–20 term was dominated by the 15 March 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks (and the subsequent firearms reforms), the 2019 Whakaari
/ White Island eruption and, from March 2020, the **COVID-19 pandemic**. New Zealand's elimination strategy, a seven-week national
lockdown and a near-closed border were popular, and Ardern's approval soared. National changed leader twice in 2020: Todd Muller
replaced Simon Bridges on 22 May, then resigned on 14 July citing health reasons, and Judith Collins took over.

The election had been set for 19 September. After community transmission re-emerged in Auckland on 11 August (Auckland back to alert
level 3), campaigns were suspended and on 17 August Ardern moved polling day to **17 October**, with Parliament dissolving on 6 September.

## Campaign and issues

- **COVID-19 recovery and border management** framed everything; ACT attacked the government's response as "demonstrably
  unsustainable" and called for a "smart border".
- **Tax.** Labour promised a new **39% top tax rate on income over $180,000** (affecting about 2% of earners, ~$550m a year); the Greens proposed a wealth tax and a **guaranteed minimum income** of $325 a week.
- **Infrastructure.** Labour's $12 billion New Zealand Upgrade Programme (announced January 2020); National promised $31 billion of
  transport projects over a decade and abolishing Auckland's regional fuel tax.
- **Energy and climate.** Labour moved its 100% renewable electricity target forward to 2030; the Greens' Clean Energy Plan aimed to end
  coal use by 2030 and proposed mandatory climate-risk disclosure for large companies.
- **Other pledges.** Labour: Matariki public holiday from 2022 (delivered). National: EVs in bus lanes, child dental care, doubling
  Serious Fraud Office funding. NZ First: keep the Provincial Growth Fund as a bottom line, cap skilled immigration, 1,000 more police.
  ACT: an employment-insurance scheme; the End of Life Choice Act on the referendum ballot was David Seymour's member's bill.
- **Coalition signals.** Under Bridges, National ruled out NZ First ("I can't trust New Zealand First"); Muller reopened the door.

### Reading the result

- **A majority from 50%.** With 7.71% of the party vote wasted on parties under the threshold (mainly NZ First, TOP, New Conservative,
  Advance NZ), Labour's 50.01% translated into 65 seats (54%).
- **Electorate sweep.** Labour won 46 of 72 electorates, taking 19 seats from National (including Ilam, Rangitata, Nelson, Whanganui,
  Northcote, Upper Harbour and Wairarapa) and Northland by just 163 votes.
- **National's lowest point.** National won only 23 electorates; its 25.58% was its worst result since 2002.
- **ACT's breakthrough** came from party votes, not deals: 7.59% gave it 9 list seats on top of Epsom.
- **Māori electorates:** Labour 6, Te Pāti Māori 1 (Waiariki, majority 836) – enough with 1.17% party vote for one extra list seat
  (Debbie Ngarewa-Packer).
- **Disinformation-era parties.** Advance NZ (co-led by former National MP Jami-Lee Ross and Billy Te Kahika), running on COVID-19
  conspiracy themes, won 0.98% and no seats.

## Electorates

72 electorates (65 general, 7 Māori) after the 2019–20 boundary review added one North Island general electorate (new or renamed seats: Banks Peninsula, Dunedin, Kaipara ki Mahurangi, Panmure-Ōtāhuhu, Port Waikato, Southland, Taieri, Takanini, Whangaparāoa). Notable:

- **Auckland Central** – Chlöe Swarbrick (Green) won by 1,068 over Labour's Helen White after National's Nikki Kaye retired.
- **Northland** – Labour's Willow-Jean Prime beat National's Matt King by 163, the closest result.
- **Epsom** – David Seymour won 9,224 votes clear of Labour's Camilla Belich; National's party vote was the only one Labour did not
  top (Labour won the most party votes in 71 of 72 electorates).
- **Waiariki** – Rawiri Waititi (Te Pāti Māori) unseated Labour's Tāmati Coffey by 836.
- **Botany** – Christopher Luxon (National) won the seat vacated by Jami-Lee Ross.

## Government formation

Labour could govern alone. On 31 October Ardern announced a **cooperation agreement** (explicitly not a coalition) with the Greens:
co-leaders James Shaw (Climate Change; Associate Environment – biodiversity) and Marama Davidson (new Minister for the Prevention of
Family and Sexual Violence; Associate Housing – homelessness) became ministers outside Cabinet, and the Greens agreed to abstain on
confidence and supply. The Sixth Labour Government's second ministry was sworn in on 6 November 2020.

## The 53rd Parliament (2020–2023)

Ardern resigned as Prime Minister in January 2023; **Chris Hipkins** was sworn in on 25 January 2023, and Ardern left Parliament in
April. National replaced Collins with **Christopher Luxon** (30 November 2021). By-elections: **Tauranga 2022** (Sam Uffindell,
National hold) and **Hamilton West 2022** (Tama Potaka, National gain, after Labour expelled Gaurav Sharma and he resigned to force
the contest). In 2023 Meka Whaitiri left Labour for Te Pāti Māori and Elizabeth Kerekere left the Greens; both sat as independents.
The term also included the 2022 Parliament-grounds protest/occupation, Three Waters reform, the 2023 Auckland floods and Cyclone
Gabrielle.

## What changed

1. MMP produced its first single-party majority – showing it is possible, but only with ~50% of the vote and a high wasted vote.
2. ACT transformed from a one-seat Epsom party into a 10-seat party – reducing the importance of the Epsom deal.
3. NZ First was eliminated (and returned in 2023); the Greens won an electorate; Te Pāti Māori re-entered Parliament.
4. The scale of 2020 set up the scale of the 2023 swing back.
