# 2023 New Zealand general election (14 October 2023)

> Structured data: [`data/elections/2023.json`](../data/elections/2023.json) · Parliament: [`data/parliaments/54.json`](../data/parliaments/54.json).
> Tables between `GENERATED` markers are rebuilt by `tools/elections_md.py`.

## At a glance

- **Change of government:** Labour (Chris Hipkins) fell from 65 seats to **34** (26.92%, −23.09 pp) – the worst defeat of a sitting
  government under MMP. National (Christopher Luxon) became the largest party with 38.08% and **48 seats** (49 after Port Waikato).
- **Government:** the first **three-party coalition** under MMP – **National–ACT–NZ First** – with separate coalition agreements
  signed 24 Nov 2023 and ministers sworn in **27 Nov 2023**. 68 of 123 seats.
- **Minor parties grew:** Greens 11.61% (15 seats, their best result, plus three electorates: Auckland Central, Wellington Central,
  Rongotai); ACT 8.64% (11 seats, and Brooke van Velden won Tāmaki); NZ First returned with 6.09% (8 seats).
- **Te Pāti Māori** won **six of seven Māori electorates** on 3.08% of the party vote – two overhang seats.
- **The biggest Parliament under MMP: 123 MPs.** ACT's Port Waikato candidate Neil Christensen died during the campaign, so the
  Port Waikato electorate vote was cancelled and a by-election held on 25 Nov 2023; National's Andrew Bayly (already elected from the
  list) won, Nancy Lu came in from National's list, and the House gained a third overhang seat.
- **Two-party vote** (National + Labour) was 65.0%, the lowest since 2002. **Turnout:** 78.20% (party vote).

## Context

Labour's 2020 majority was eroded by the long tail of COVID-19 (Auckland's 2021 Delta lockdown, vaccine mandates and the 2022
Parliament-grounds occupation), high inflation and interest rates, a cost-of-living squeeze, and controversy over **Three Waters**
reform and **co-governance**. Labour lost the 2022 Hamilton West by-election to National. Jacinda Ardern resigned in January 2023 and
Chris Hipkins became PM on 25 January. National had changed leader in 2021, Christopher Luxon
replacing Judith Collins on 30 November 2021.

## Campaign and issues

A Vote Compass survey found the top issues in general electorates were the cost of living (28%), the economy (17%), healthcare (14%),
crime (9%) and the environment (8%); in the Māori electorates, cost of living (35%), Māori issues (15%), the economy (14%).

**National – "Get our country back on track."** $14.6 billion of income-tax cuts for "the squeezed middle" (to be funded by public-
service cuts and new taxes on foreign home buyers, offshore gambling operators and commercial buildings – the foreign buyer tax was dropped in the coalition deal with NZ First); repeal of Three Waters and the "RMA 2.0" laws; a
100-day plan (scrapping the Auckland regional fuel tax, banning gang patches, restoring 90-day trials, banning cellphones in schools);
a $24 billion transport package with 13 "roads of national significance"; a third medical school at Waikato; ending the Clean Car
Discount; reversing blanket speed-limit reductions; a "traffic light" system for Jobseeker beneficiaries; ending the GM ban.

**Labour – "In It For You."** Removing GST from fresh and frozen fruit and vegetables (criticised by many economists); boosting
Working for Families; free dental care for under-30s from 2025; 300 more frontline police; 6,000 more state houses; keeping the
superannuation age at 65; ruling out a capital gains tax (Hipkins, 12 July); keeping free school lunches; a ram-raid
offence; a $1 billion boost for Pharmac.

**Greens – "The Time Is Now."** A wealth tax on net assets over $2 million, a 45% top rate, a 33% company rate and income-tax cuts for
those under $125,000; a guaranteed minimum income of $385 a week; rent controls and a rental warrant of fitness; 35,000 public homes;
free dental care; Hoki Whenua Mai (returning confiscated land). Ran "two-tick" campaigns in Auckland Central, Mount Albert, Rongotai and
Wellington Central.

**ACT.** A Ministry of Regulation and Regulatory Standards Bill; legislating the **principles of the Treaty of
Waitangi** with a referendum; abolishing Māori wards; repealing the Zero Carbon Act; three-strikes law restored; lowering the youth
justice age to 17; abolishing Fair Pay Agreements; abolishing the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, Human Rights Commission and Ministry
for Women; two-tick campaigns in Epsom and Tāmaki.

**NZ First – "Let's take back our country."** Opposing "racist separatism" and co-governance; English names for government
departments and making English an official language; removing GST on basic foods; breaking the supermarket duopoly and taking on
Australian-owned banks; a COVID-19 inquiry; moving the Ports of Auckland to Northport; a "gang prison"; transgender bathrooms and
sports policy.

**Te Pāti Māori** – no income tax under $30,000, a 48% rate over $300,000, a wealth tax, a 33% company rate; replacing Oranga
Tamariki with a Mokopuna Māori Authority; a Māori parliament and entrenched Māori seats. **TOP** – UBI and land tax, the "Teal Deal"
for under-30s, leader Raf Manji's bid for Ilam.

**The electorate-deal question.** National ended its "teacup" understanding with ACT and actively contested Epsom (28 Aug); Labour
ruled out a deal with the Greens in tight seats; Luxon said (25 Sep) he could work with NZ First after the election, and Sir John Key
urged voters to give National their party vote to avoid a hung Parliament.

**Co-governance and the Treaty** were the most polarising issues; National ruled out working with Te Pāti Māori (May 2023).

### Reading the result

- **Seat arithmetic.** National 48 + ACT 11 = 59 on the official count, short of 62 needed in a 122-seat House – so NZ First (8) was
  needed. After Port Waikato: 49 + 11 + 8 = 68 of 123.
- **Overhang.** Te Pāti Māori's six electorates exceeded its four-seat entitlement (2 overhang); the Port Waikato by-election added a
  third. This 123-member House is the largest under MMP.
- **Ticket-splitting.** National won 43.47% of electorate votes vs 38.08% party votes; the Greens and ACT won more electorates than
  ever (3 and 2); Te Pāti Māori's electorate vote (3.89%) was larger than its party vote (3.08%), consistent with Māori-roll voters
  splitting electorate TPM / party Labour or Green.
- **Recounts.** Judicial recounts changed results slightly: Mount Albert (Helen White, Labour, by 18), Nelson (Rachel Boyack, Labour,
  by 26) and Tāmaki Makaurau (Takutai Tarsh Kemp, TPM, by 42) were the three closest seats in the country.
- **Wasted vote.** 5.58% of valid party votes (TOP 2.22%, NZ Loyal 1.21% and many small parties) won no seats.

## Electorates

72 electorates (65 general, 7 Māori). National took 21 electorates from Labour (see the "changed party" list below); Labour's
electorate tally collapsed from 46 to 17, while Labour held Nelson by 26 and Mount Albert by 18. Highlights:

- **Te Pāti Māori** took Hauraki-Waikato (21-year-old Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke defeating Foreign Minister Nanaia Mahuta),
  Te Tai Hauāuru (Debbie Ngarewa-Packer), Te Tai Tokerau (Mariameno Kapa-Kingi by 517 over Kelvin Davis), Te Tai Tonga (Tākuta Ferris)
  and Tāmaki Makaurau (Takutai Tarsh Kemp by 42 over Peeni Henare), and held Waiariki (Rawiri Waititi, majority 15,891).
  Labour kept **Ikaroa-Rāwhiti** (Cushla Tangaere-Manuel) against Meka Whaitiri, who had defected to TPM.
- **Greens:** Chlöe Swarbrick held Auckland Central; Tamatha Paul won **Wellington Central** and Julie Anne Genter **Rongotai** –
  the first time the Greens held three electorates.
- **ACT:** Brooke van Velden won **Tāmaki** from National; David Seymour held Epsom (8,142) despite National contesting it.
- **Ōhāriu:** Labour's Greg O'Connor held off Finance-spokesperson Nicola Willis (1,260).
- **Port Waikato:** by-election 25 Nov 2023 (see above).

## Government formation

National began talks with ACT and NZ First after election night; the official results (3 Nov) removed the option of a two-party
National–ACT majority. ACT and NZ First held their first direct talks on 8 Nov. The caretaker Labour government stayed on while talks
continued. On 23 Nov the three leaders finalised the deal in Wellington; the **coalition agreements** (National–ACT and National–NZ
First, plus a shared programme) were published on **24 November 2023**, and Luxon and his ministers were sworn in on
**27 November 2023**. Key elements: ACT's **Treaty Principles Bill** would be introduced, but the government would not back ACT's referendum (National and
NZ First supported the bill only through its first reading); ACT's Regulatory Standards Bill (passed into law in Nov 2025, with NZ First
later pledging to repeal it); repeal of Three Waters (passed Feb 2024), Fair Pay Agreements, Auckland light rail and the Māori Health
Authority; Māori wards to face local referendums; English prioritised in government departments; the COVID-19 Royal Commission's scope
widened (NZ First); National's foreign-buyer tax dropped; and the Deputy Prime Minister role shared – Winston Peters, then David Seymour
from 31 May 2025.

## The 54th Parliament (2023–2026)

A turbulent term with many changes (details in [`data/parliaments/54.json`](../data/parliaments/54.json)):

- **Greens:** Golriz Ghahraman resigned (Jan 2024, shoplifting charges); Efeso Collins died (Feb 2024); James Shaw retired (May 2024);
  **Darleen Tana** left the party (Jul 2024) and became the first MP expelled under the 2018 "waka-jumping" law (22 Oct 2024);
  Benjamin Doyle resigned (Oct 2025).
- **Labour:** Andrew Little, Rino Tirikatene, Kelvin Davis, Grant Robertson, David Parker, Adrian Rurawhe and Peeni Henare all resigned
  and were replaced from the list.
- **Te Pāti Māori:** Takutai Tarsh Kemp died (26 Jun 2025) and **Oriini Kaipara** held **Tāmaki Makaurau** at the 6 Sep 2025
  by-election. In Nov 2025 the party **expelled Tākuta Ferris and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi**; Kapa-Kingi's expulsion was later ruled
  unlawful by the High Court (sources differ on the date of reinstatement: 5 Dec 2025 in Parliament's record per Wikipedia's
  54th-Parliament table vs the 10 Mar 2026 judgment), and on 11 May 2026 she left to found the **Te Tai Tokerau Party**. At dissolution
  TPM had 4 MPs and there were 2 independents.
- **National:** Judith Collins resigned (May 2026) to become President of the Law Commission; no by-election (too close to the
  election). Luxon survived leadership votes in April and August 2026.
- **NZ First:** Tanya Unkovich resigned (Jun 2025), replaced by David Wilson.

## What changed

1. The swing from 2020 was the largest under MMP; Labour's vote nearly halved.
2. MMP's first three-party coalition, and a return to formal written coalition agreements with policy "bottom lines".
3. Te Pāti Māori's Māori-seat sweep produced the largest overhang under MMP and a 123-seat House – reigniting debate about the
   overhang rule (the 2012 MMP review had recommended abolishing it).
4. Minor parties (Greens, ACT, NZ First, TPM) together won 29.4% of the party vote, the most of any election in this archive.

## The record being judged: the 54th Parliament (2023–26)

The National–ACT–NZ First coalition (68 of 123 seats at the start, 67 of 122 at dissolution) made sweeping changes, many under
urgency. Among them: repeal of Fair Pay Agreements, the Clean Car Discount, Three Waters and Labour's RMA replacement laws; disestablishing
the Māori Health Authority; repealing the smokefree generation law; restoring interest deductibility for landlords and a two-year
bright-line test; road-user charges for EVs; reinstating 90-day trials, three-strikes and Māori-ward referendums; the **Fast-track
Approvals Act 2024**; **Local Water Done Well**; the **Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025** (pay-equity changes, opposed by all opposition
parties); repealing the offshore oil-and-gas exploration ban; and the **Regulatory Standards Act 2025**. ACT's **Treaty Principles
Bill** drew the November 2024 hīkoi to Parliament and was voted down at its second reading on 10 April 2025, National and NZ First
having supported it only to select committee. The rotating deputy prime ministership passed from Winston Peters to David Seymour on
31 May 2025.

Inside Parliament, Te Pāti Māori went from six MPs to four (Kemp's death and the Tāmaki Makaurau by-election win by Oriini Kaipara;
the expulsions of Tākuta Ferris and Mariameno Kapa-Kingi), the Greens lost or replaced five MPs, and Luxon faced two leadership
votes in 2026 (April and August). From March 2026 the Iran war and closure of the Strait of Hormuz drove a fuel-price shock.

## Campaign issues

An Ipsos Issues Monitor (May 2026) found the top concerns were the **cost of living/inflation (61%)**, healthcare (39%), the economy
(33%), petrol prices (26%), housing (21%) and unemployment (19%). Respondents rated Labour most capable on inflation, health, petrol,
housing, jobs, poverty and education; National on the economy and crime; the Greens on climate change. A September Ipsos survey found
64% support for the Greens' proposed 2.5% wealth tax on assets over $10 million (excl. family homes) and 45% for Labour's capital gains
tax.

Other prominent issues: **supermarket duopoly** (five parties have break-up or competition policies); energy prices and the fuel
shock; Treaty/co-governance and the future of the Māori seats; immigration and citizenship; law and order; KiwiSaver and retirement
savings; misinformation; and **strategic voting** (Te Pāti Māori urging electorate-TPM/party-Labour-or-Green; National urging no vote
splitting; a businessman's site urging right-leaning voters to give National the electorate vote and ACT/NZ First the party vote).

## Main parties' key promises (summary)

Detailed policy texts are in each party folder (`parties/<party>/policies/`); the summaries below are from campaign coverage
collected on Wikipedia's 2026 election article.

- **National** (Luxon; "ten commitments", launched 27 Sep): no new taxes and three budget-responsibility rules (delaying further tax
  cuts); **compulsory KiwiSaver** with default contributions rising to 6% by 2032 and automatic enrolment of babies; paid parental
  leave extended from 26 to 30 weeks; replacing NCEA; easier 5% deposits for first-home buyers; lower student-loan repayment rates for
  borrowers at home; splitting Foodstuffs to break the supermarket duopoly; $604m for Pharmac and expanded cancer screening, funded by
  cutting non-Pacific aid; welfare savings ($585m) and drug-testing of beneficiaries; referendums on MMP and a four-year term; ruled out
  working with TOP.
- **Labour** (Hipkins; "Better Starts Now"): a **capital gains tax** on property (excl. family home and farms) to fund **three free
  GP visits a year**; a **NZ Future Fund**; repeal of the Regulatory Standards Act in 100 days; forcing supermarkets to separate
  wholesale and retail; public transport caps ($20/week in the main cities); 10% student-loan write-off; restoring pay equity; a "fair
  go" consumer law; debt to 20% of GDP and a Parliamentary Budget Office; recognising Palestine; an under-16 social media ban to select
  committee. Labour and the Greens announced at Waitangi (Feb 2026) that they would work together in government.
- **Greens** (Davidson & Swarbrick; "For All of Us"): wealth, inheritance and corporate taxes with a tax-free band under $10,000 and
  higher rates over $160,000; 40,000 social homes and 2% rent-rise caps; a state-owned **KiwiMart** supermarket chain; Kiwipower
  renewable energy entity; free/cheap public transport and $4b intercity rail; revoking fast-track mining consents; restoring the
  previous school-lunch programme and pay equity.
- **ACT** (Seymour): cutting government spending and merging ministries; ending "race-based hiring"; entrenching equal rights, rule of
  law and parliamentary sovereignty; abolishing the Climate Change Commission and net-zero target; dissolving the Waitangi Tribunal
  once historical claims are settled; progressively raising the retirement age; a three-year minimum-wage cap; tighter immigration
  and welfare rules for residents; opposes breaking up supermarkets.
- **NZ First** (Peters): breaking up Foodstuffs; splitting the "gentailer" power companies; nationalising BNZ to merge with Kiwibank;
  a Crown-funded KiwiSaver for newborns and a $5,000/year "Kiwi Kids Grant"; voting and super restricted to citizens; a referendum on
  the Māori seats and on capping resident visas at 20,000; mining on conservation land; repealing the Regulatory Standards Act it voted
  for; ruled out working with Labour.
- **Te Pāti Māori** (Ngarewa-Packer & Waititi): a 48% top tax rate, wealth/land-banking/vacant-house taxes; a Te Tiriti Commission and
  binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations; abolishing prisons by 2040; standing in all seven Māori seats.
- **TOP** (Qiulae Wong): land value tax funding a means-tested "citizen's income"; citizens' assemblies; lobbying and donations reform;
  bottom-trawling ban.

**Reading it.** The two big parties alternate in long arcs: National held 44–47% for three elections (2008–2017), collapsed to

in government again in 2023.

## 3. Turnout, overhang and the "wasted" vote

<!-- GENERATED:turnout START -->
| Year | Enrolled | Votes cast | Turnout % | Overhang | Parties winning seats | Parties on ballot (party vote) | 'Wasted' party vote % |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2008 | 2,990,759 | 2,376,480 | 79.46 | 2 | 7 | 19 | 6.55 |
| 2011 | 3,070,847 | 2,278,989 | 74.21 | 1 | 8 | 13 | 3.37 |
| 2014 | 3,140,417 | 2,446,297 | 77.9 | 1 | 7 | 15 | 6.24 |
| 2017 | 3,298,009 | 2,630,173 | 79.75 | 0 | 5 | 16 | 4.68 |
| 2020 | 3,549,580 | 2,919,073 | 82.24 | 0 | 5 | 17 | 7.8 |
| 2023 | 3,688,292 | 2,884,111 | 78.2 | 3 | 6 | 17 | 5.58 |
<!-- GENERATED:turnout END -->

- **Turnout** (votes cast ÷ enrolled) ranged from 74.21% (2011, the lowest since 1887) to 82.24% (2020). Turnout of the *eligible*
  population is lower because not everyone enrols; youth enrolment fell to 53% by mid-2026 before a late push (65.5% of 18–24s by
  15 Oct 2026, per the Electoral Commission as reported on Wikipedia).
- **The 5% threshold and the wasted vote.** "Wasted" here = party votes for parties that won no seats, as a share of valid party
  votes. It peaked at **7.8% in 2020** (NZ First 2.6%, TOP 1.5%, New Conservative 1.5%, Advance NZ 1.0%) and was 6.2–6.6% in 2008
  and 2014 (NZ First 4.07% in 2008; the Conservatives 3.97% in 2014). Wasted votes are redistributed in effect to parties that did
  qualify – one reason Labour's 50.0% in 2020 produced 54% of the seats. The Electoral Commission's 2012 MMP review recommended
  lowering the threshold to 4%; it was never legislated.
- **Overhang.** Overhang seats arise when a party wins more electorates than its party-vote entitlement: the Māori Party in 2008
  (+2) and 2011 (+1), United Future in 2014 (+1), and Te Pāti Māori in 2023 (+2) plus the Port Waikato by-election (+1), giving a
  **123-seat House** – the largest under MMP. 2017 and 2020 had none.

## 4. The two-party vote and swing

<!-- GENERATED:two-party START -->
| Election | National % | Labour % | Nat–Lab gap (pp) | Two-party combined % | Largest party | Govt formed by |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 2008 | 44.93 | 33.99 | +10.94 | 78.92 | National | National |
| 2011 | 47.31 | 27.48 | +19.83 | 74.79 | National | National |
| 2014 | 47.04 | 25.13 | +21.91 | 72.17 | National | National |

- The combined National+Labour vote was highest in 2017 (81.3%) and lowest in 2023 (65.0%, the lowest since 2002), when minor
  parties (Greens, ACT, NZ First, TPM) won 29.4%.
- **Swing.** 2017→2020 was a ~19 pp National→Labour swing on the party vote; 2020→2023 a 12.5 pp swing back to National and a 23 pp fall
  for Labour – the largest defeat of a sitting government under MMP. The 2017 election is the only one here where the largest party
  (National) did not form the government.
- **Rise-and-fall cycle.** Each major party has followed a "three-term" pattern: Fifth National Government 2008–17 (three terms);
  Sixth Labour Government 2017–23 (two terms, ending in a landslide defeat after a landslide win). Polling through 2025–26 suggests the
  2023 coalition faces a close contest after one term (see §8).

## 6. Electorate deals ("coat-tailing"): Epsom and Ōhāriu

Under MMP a party that wins **one electorate** gets its full party-vote share of seats even below 5%. National repeatedly signalled to
its Epsom (and Ōhāriu) voters to back ACT's (and United Future's) candidate – the 2011 "tea tape" meeting is the best-known example.

<!-- GENERATED:deals START -->
| Year | Epsom winner (majority) | Ōhāriu/Ohariu winner (majority) | Party vote of the winner's party | Seats the deal delivered |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2008 | Rodney Hide (ACT, 12,882) | Peter Dunne (United Future, 1,006) | ACT 3.65%; United Future 0.87% | ACT 5, UF 1 |
| 2011 | John Banks (ACT, 2,261) | Peter Dunne (United Future, 1,392) | ACT 1.07%; United Future 0.6% | ACT 1, UF 1 |
| 2014 | David Seymour (ACT, 4,250) | Peter Dunne (United Future, 710) | ACT 0.69%; United Future 0.22% | ACT 1, UF 1 |
| 2017 | David Seymour (ACT, 5,519) | Greg O'Connor (Labour, 1,051) | ACT 0.5%; United Future 0.07% | ACT 1, UF 0 |
| 2020 | David Seymour (ACT, 9,224) | Greg O'Connor (Labour, 11,961) | ACT 7.59% | ACT 10 |
| 2023 | David Seymour (ACT, 8,142) | Greg O'Connor (Labour, 1,260) | ACT 8.64% | ACT 11 |
<!-- GENERATED:deals END -->

- In 2008 Epsom brought in **four extra ACT list MPs** (3.65% → 5 seats) – the clearest coat-tail effect in this period.
- 2011–2017 ACT's party vote was so low that Epsom delivered only the electorate MP; United Future's Ōhāriu seat in 2014 was an overhang.
- 2014's attempted coat-tail for Internet MANA failed when Labour's Kelvin Davis beat Hone Harawira in Te Tai Tokerau (with public
  endorsements from John Key and Winston Peters).
- From 2020 ACT no longer needed Epsom; in 2023 National formally contested it, and Seymour still won by 8,142.
- The 2012 MMP review recommended abolishing the one-electorate threshold; Parliament did not act.

# Political alignment ("compass") test: how it works

The compass data is in [`data/guide/compass.json`](../data/guide/compass.json) (the 36 items, axes and scoring rules) and [`data/guide/compass-parties.json`](../data/guide/compass-parties.json) (where the parties sit, from published data and from our own coding). Both are built by `tools/compass_build.py` from `tools/compass_items.py`, `tools/compass_party_coding.py` and `tools/compass_published.py`; the downloaded source material is in `raw/compass/` and the small extracts there are regenerated by `tools/compass_extract.py`.

Unlike the ["Find your match" quiz](quiz-method.md), which asks about concrete 2026 New Zealand dividing lines, the compass asks about **general political and social values**: how far the state should go in the economy, how much weight to put on order and tradition against personal freedom, and how far you trust politicians at all. It then shows where you sit on two standard scholarly axes (plus a secondary populism axis) and where the New Zealand parties sit on the same map.

It is a description of your values, not a voting recommendation. A two-dimensional map flattens politics (see section 7) and the parties' points are estimates with real uncertainty.

## 1. Where the questions come from, and why we may use them

Every item is taken verbatim (or with a minimal, recorded adaptation) from an instrument that is either openly licensed or a standard public survey questionnaire. We did **not** use the statement sets of politicalcompass.org, 8values, 9Axes, SapplyValues or similar sites: those are proprietary, unvalidated, and their items mix several dimensions.

| Instrument | Items used | Why | Licence / terms | Where we got it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Social and Economic Conservatism Scale (SECS)**, Everett 2013, *PLoS ONE* 8(12): e82131 | all 12 (7 social, 5 economic) | The only short, validated two-factor conservatism scale with published psychometrics (alpha .88 overall; .87 social; .70 economic). Items are single issue words rated on a feeling thermometer, which avoids the double-barrelled statements common in online compasses. | **CC0** public-domain dedication (stated in the article) | [doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0082131](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0082131); archived `raw/compass/secs_everett2013.html` |
| **Very Short Authoritarianism (VSA) scale**, Bizumic & Duckitt 2018, *J. Social and Political Psychology* 6(1) | all 6 | Six-item, balanced (3 pro-trait, 3 con-trait) measure of right-wing authoritarianism covering Duckitt's three facets (submission, conventionalism, aggression); validated in four samples including New Zealand. It correlates .94 with the 18-item ACT scale. | **CC BY 4.0** | [doi:10.5964/jspp.v6i1.835](https://doi.org/10.5964/jspp.v6i1.835); archived `raw/compass/vsa_bizumic2018.html` |
| **CSES Module 5 (2016-21) "Democracy Divided? People, Politicians and the Politics of Populism"** | Q04a-g (7 elite items), Q05b (majority vs minority rights), Q05c-d (immigration), Q08 (reduce income differences) | The populism battery is the international standard, fielded in 40+ elections including the 2017 and 2020 NZES, so New Zealand population distributions exist. Q08 is identical to ESS B33 and NZES C6a. | Public questionnaire; data free for research with citation | [cses5_Questionnaire.txt](https://cses.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/cses5_Questionnaire.txt); archived in `raw/compass/` |
| **World Values Survey Wave 7 (2017-22)** | Q106-Q109 (economic values) | The classic cross-national economic-values items (equality vs incentives; private vs state ownership; government vs individual responsibility; competition good vs harmful). | Questionnaire and data free for non-commercial research with citation | [WVS documentation](https://www.worldvaluessurvey.org/WVSDocumentationWV7.jsp); copy used: Wave 7 master questionnaire as fielded in Great Britain (IHSN 12279), `raw/compass/wvs7_master_questionnaire.pdf` |
| **European Social Survey** core questionnaire | B34 "Gay men and lesbians should be free to live their own life as they wish" (freehms) | A single, widely benchmarked social-liberalism item asked in every ESS round since 2002. | ESS documentation **CC BY-SA 4.0**; data CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | [ESS9 source questionnaire](https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/docs/round9/fieldwork/source/ESS9_source_questionnaires.pdf); archived `raw/compass/ESS9_source_questionnaires.pdf` |
| **New Zealand Election Study 2023** questionnaire | C6c "Privatisation of state-owned enterprises has gone too far"; C12e "Big business in New Zealand has too much power" | Long-running NZES economic-values items, so the compass can later be benchmarked against the NZ electorate. | Publicly posted questionnaire; cited as a research instrument (unit-record data not used) | [2023 NZES questionnaire](https://www.nzes.net/files/2024/03/2023-NZESFinal-d23f98922870a844.pdf); archived `raw/compass/nzes2023_questionnaire.pdf` |

What we **did not** use, and why:

- *Akkerman, Mudde & Zaslove (2014)* six-item populism scale: published in *Comparative Political Studies* (Sage, not open access). The CSES Module 5 battery was designed by the same research community, covers the same three components (people-centrism, anti-elitism, popular sovereignty) and is public, so we used it instead. The same applies to the Castanho Silva et al. (2020) short scale.
- *ISSP Role of Government (2016)* "should it be the government's responsibility to..." items: the official source questionnaire sits behind GESIS registration and we could not obtain a verified copy, so we did not reproduce the wording from memory.
- *NZES Treaty / biculturalism items* (C9, C11, C12d, C12i): these would form a fourth, New Zealand-specific axis. We left them out of this general test because the quiz already covers Te Tiriti issues concretely; they could be added later as a clearly separated optional axis.

### Adaptations (all recorded per item in `compass.json`)

- SECS items are feeling-thermometer words ("How positive or negative do you feel about: Abortion"). Everett used 0-100; we use a 5-point very negative to very positive scale mapped to -2..+2, and report an approximate 0-100 subscale score as 50 + 12.5 x mean (see scoring). The SECS item "Gun ownership" is American in flavour, as Everett acknowledges; we keep it so the economic subscale is complete and flag it in the item note.
- WVS Q106-Q109 are 1-10 bipolar scales between two statements. We present one pole as a 5-point agree/disagree statement and record the opposing pole in the item note.
- CSES "[COUNTRY]" is replaced by "New Zealand".
- VSA items were fielded on a 9-point scale; we use 5 points. One VSA item is kept with the typographical slip in the published appendix ("if we are going preserve law and order") because the licence condition is faithful reproduction with attribution; the app may silently correct it.

## 2. The axes and their scientific basis

**Economic left-right** (12 items; 6 keyed each way). Left = redistribution, public ownership, government responsibility; right = markets, limited government, fiscal restraint. This is the "lrecon" dimension of the Chapel Hill Expert Survey and the Global Party Survey (Norris 2020, V4), and the first dimension in Hooghe, Marks and Wilson (2002).

**Social: GAL-TAN / libertarian-authoritarian** (16 items; 10 keyed TAN, 6 keyed GAL). GAL = green, alternative, libertarian: personal freedom, pluralism, openness to immigrants and minorities; TAN = traditional, authoritarian, nationalist: order, tradition, national culture (Hooghe, Marks & Wilson 2002; Kitschelt 1994; CHES "galtan"; GPS V6). The VSA supplies the authoritarianism core (Duckitt's submission, conventionalism, aggression), SECS the traditionalism items, and the ESS and CSES items the tolerance and immigration components.

**Populism / anti-establishment** (8 items; 7 keyed populist, 1 reverse). Mudde's (2004) "thin ideology" that society is divided into the pure people and the corrupt elite, and that politics should express the will of the people; measured with the CSES elite battery plus the anti-pluralism item. Because the CSES items are nearly all worded in the populist direction, acquiescence bias cannot be balanced out on this axis, so the app should present it as a **secondary, indicative** axis, not as a third coordinate of equal standing.

### Validity and the limits of two dimensions

- Political attitudes are at least two-dimensional in most electorates, and the two dimensions are only loosely related: economic and social conservatism correlate modestly in mass publics, and many people are "cross-pressured" (Feldman & Johnston 2014; Malka, Lelkes & Soto 2019; Lefkofridi, Wagner & Willmann 2014). A single left-right score would hide this, which is why we show two axes.
- Even two axes flatten real structure: immigration, environment, religion and Te Tiriti do not load cleanly on either axis in New Zealand (Vowles, Coffé & Curtin 2017 on the 2014 NZES; Vowles et al. on 2017 and 2020). Our social axis bundles authority, tradition and openness because that is how GAL-TAN is defined, but a respondent can be libertarian on crime and restrictive on immigration; the per-subscale scores show this.
- Short scales are less reliable than long ones. The VSA's reported alpha is .71 in the authors' data and .54-.66 in replications; the SECS economic subscale is .70. We therefore report an uncertainty band around each point rather than a dot alone.
- The economic items were written for cross-national surveys and for the US (SECS). Wording such as "Gun ownership" or "Limited government" has a different resonance in New Zealand; we kept the items for comparability and flag them.
- The test measures stated values, not vote choice. Nothing in it is a party cue (no party names, no NZ policy specifics), which is intended, but it also means the party points come from a different kind of evidence than the user's point (section 5).

## 3. Scoring

Responses are -2 (strongly disagree / very negative) to +2 (strongly agree / very positive); a skipped item is null.

```
keyed_i   = direction_i x response_i                 (+2 always = right / TAN / populist pole)
axis      = 5 x mean(keyed_i over answered items)     (range -10 .. +10)
```

Minimum items answered to show an axis: economic 6 of 12, social 8 of 16, populism 4 of 8. Below that the app shows "not enough answers" for that axis.

**Uncertainty.** `half_width = max(1.0, 1.96 x 5 x sd(keyed_i) / sqrt(n))`, where `sd` is the sample standard deviation of the keyed scores on that axis and `n` the number answered. The floor of 1.0 says that even a complete, internally consistent set of 5-point answers cannot locate a person more finely than about a unit on a 20-unit axis. The app shows the point with a +/- half-width band and the text "based on n of N items".

**Subscales.** Each item is tagged (SECS economic, SECS social, VSA authoritarianism, CSES populism, CSES out-group, WVS economic values, ESS, NZES). A subscale score is 5 x mean(keyed) over the answered items with that tag, shown when at least half of its items were answered. For SECS we also give Everett's 0-100 metric approximately as `50 + 12.5 x mean(keyed)` (so the 5-point version spans 25-75 of the original thermometer).

**Acquiescence.** Half of the economic items and six of the sixteen social items are reverse-keyed, so a respondent who agrees with everything lands near the centre of those axes rather than at an extreme. The populism battery cannot be balanced (see above).

## 4. Where the parties sit: published data

`compass-parties.json` keeps every published value on its **original scale** with the source's own scale definition, and adds a stated rescaling to -10..+10 (`(x - 5) x 2` for 0-10 scales; `(osp - 3) x 10/3` for V-Party's 0-6 ordinal economic scale; `(index - 0.5) x 20` for V-Party's 0-1 populism index). Nothing is converted silently.

| Source | What it is | NZ coverage | Scales | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Party Survey 2019** (Norris, Harvard Dataverse) | 12 country experts rated each party | National, Labour, Green, ACT, NZ First (reference election 2017). Māori Party and TOP not rated. | V4 economic left-right 0-10; V6 social liberal-conservative 0-10; V8 populist rhetoric 0-10; plus immigration, environment, nationalism, liberal democracy | CC0 |
| **V-Party v2** (V-Dem Institute, 2022) | Expert coding of parties per election | National, Labour, Green, NZ First to 2017; ACT only to 2002; no Māori Party, TOP or later minor parties | v2pariglef economic left-right (interval, and 0-6 ordinal); welfare, LGBT equality, religious principles, immigration, cultural superiority (0-4); populism and anti-pluralism indices (0-1) | free with citation (no CC licence stated) |
| **CSES Module 5** | The NZES collaborator's expert left-right placement of each party (E5018) and respondents' mean placements (E3019) | 2017: National, Labour, NZ First, Green, TOP, Māori Party, ACT, Mana; 2020: Labour, National, Green, ACT, NZ First, TOP, New Conservative, Māori Party | 0 left .. 10 right (general left-right, not economic only) | free with citation |
| **NZES 2020 and 2023** voter placements | Weighted means computed from the published frequency tables of "Where would you place these parties ... 0 most left .. 10 most right" | 2023: Labour, National, Green, ACT, NZ First, Te Pāti Māori, TOP; 2020 adds New Conservative | 0-10 general left-right; "don't know" shares are shown (18% for the big parties, 57% for TOP in 2023) | public tables; unit-record data not used |
| **ParlGov** | Composite of the Castles-Mair (1984), Huber-Inglehart (1995) and Benoit-Laver (2006) expert surveys | Expert-based values for National, Labour, Green, ACT, NZ First, Alliance; family means (flagged) for TOP, Conservative/New Conservative | left_right, state_market, liberty_authority 0-10 | CC0 (2024 release) |

Not available: the **Manifesto Project (MARPOR) RILE** scores need a registered API key we could not use from this environment, and no published NZ 2017-2023 RILE table was found; **Vote Compass NZ** (Vox Pop Labs/1News) shows party coordinates only inside the application and does not publish them; **CHES** does not cover New Zealand. These are recorded in `not_retrieved` with the reason.

The published placements have three limits worth stating plainly. They are **old** (GPS and V-Party describe the parties at the 2017 election; ParlGov's latest expert input is 2003-04). They **cover few parties** (five for GPS; none of the 2026 minor parties). And most of them measure a **general** left-right position, which is not the same as our economic axis; we label those values `general_left_right` and never plot them as if they were economic scores.

## 5. Where the parties sit: our own coding ("the party takes the test")

For each of the 17 parties registered for the 2026 election we answered every compass item as the party would, strictly from evidence, in `tools/compass_party_coding.py`:

- **Sources, in order:** (1) the party's 2026 policy documents archived verbatim under `parties/<slug>/policies/documents/` and its policy.nz entries; (2) recorded parliamentary votes (Abortion Legislation Act 2020, Marriage Amendment Act 2013, Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022, Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Act 2024, Treaty Principles Bill 2025, Regulatory Standards Act 2025), attributed to a party only when its whole caucus or a clear majority voted one way; (3) on-record statements by the leader or MPs (speeches republished on Scoop, press releases, news reports).
- **Cells** are `{position -2..+2, evidence, source_url, confidence}`. `position` is relative to the item text; the direction key is applied afterwards. `confidence` is `high` (explicit policy, vote or leader statement on the substance), `medium` (a clear position needing one inferential step, e.g. a surplus rule read as "fiscal responsibility"), or `low` (indirect, dated or mixed signals).
- **Null means no evidence.** We did not infer a position from a party's general philosophy, and two VSA items of private morality ("defy authority", "premarital sex") are null for every party because no party takes a public stance on them. Thermometer items were coded only where a party expresses an attitude to the object itself (e.g. "Religion" is coded for Vision NZ and the Conservatives, not for parties that merely protect religion from hate speech).
- **Mixed records get 0** with the conflict described (for example NZ First on "government should take more responsibility": "a hand up in times of need" against calling a universal basic income "communism").
- Party axis scores use **exactly the same formula** as the user test, over the coded items, with the same minimum-items rule and uncertainty band, so a user's point and a party's point are comparable. The number of coded items and the confidence mix are stored so the app can grey out thin estimates (for example Legalise Cannabis and Free Palestine have too few codable items to be placed at all).

**Member and MP surveys.** The brief asked us to use candidate or MP survey data where it exists. The NZES has run candidate surveys (the Comparative Candidates Survey, 2008-2017), but their party-level value scores are not published in a form we could cite, and no 2023 or 2026 MP values survey was found. The party points are therefore **document-and-vote based** and describe the party's public programme, not the private values of its members. The only member-level evidence used is roll-call behaviour on conscience votes, which is explicitly attributed.

### Our coding against the published data

The `comparison` block for each party gives our axis scores next to the rescaled GPS 2019, ParlGov and V-Party values and the difference (Appendix C). Three patterns stand out and are worth showing users:

- **Ordering agrees, levels are more polarised in our coding.** On both main axes our coding ranks the five GPS-rated parties in the same order as the experts (ACT, National, NZ First, Labour, Green on the economic axis; Vision NZ-style conservatives, NZ First, National, ACT, Labour, Green on the social axis), but our scores sit further from the centre (for example the Greens at about -7.5 economic / -9.5 social against the experts' -4.4 / -6.2). This is a known property of coding manifestos item by item: a party document states positions in clear "strongly agree" terms, while experts average over behaviour in office and coalition compromises. Treat our party points as the party's *programme*, the expert points as its *reputation*.
- On the **social axis** the two sources agree closely for National, NZ First and ACT (ACT slightly liberal on social values despite being hard-line on crime; NZ First clearly conservative).
- On the **economic axis** we place **NZ First near the centre, slightly left**, where the GPS experts put it right of centre. The difference comes from the 2026 record: public ownership of assets, buying back BNZ, breaking up the supermarket duopoly and attacks on "neoliberal" privatisation all score left on our items, while its welfare and tax positions score right. V-Party's 2017 coding (also slightly left of centre) and ParlGov's composite (near centre) are closer to ours than to the GPS. Users should see both.

## 6. Reading the map

- The two main axes are economic (horizontal) and social (vertical); populism is shown as a separate bar.
- Each point has an uncertainty band. A user's band shrinks with more answers; a party's band depends on how many items it could be coded on and how consistent its coded answers are.
- Distance between a user and a party is the Euclidean distance in the economic x social plane, shown only when both have enough items on both axes. Distance is **not** a match percentage and is not comparable with the quiz's match score; the quiz measures agreement on 45 concrete 2026 issues, the compass measures proximity on two abstract value dimensions.
- Where a published placement exists, show it as a hollow marker next to our filled marker, with its source and year, so the disagreement is visible rather than averaged away.

## 7. Caveats

1. **Two dimensions flatten politics.** Environment, Te Tiriti, immigration and foreign policy each have their own structure in New Zealand; a party or voter can be anywhere on them while sharing an economic-social position with someone they disagree with profoundly.
2. **The party answers are coded from documents, not from a survey of members.** They describe what the party says it will do, weighted toward the issues it chooses to talk about. Silence is recorded as null, so parties with thin programmes have wide bands or no point.
3. **Instrument origins.** SECS is American and some items (gun ownership, limited government) carry different connotations here. VSA and the CSES battery are cross-national but short; reliabilities are modest. We cite each item's origin so a user can discount any item.
4. **The populism axis is one-sided** in wording and should be read as indicative.
5. **Published expert data are dated and sparse** (section 4).
6. **Coding judgement.** Someone else coding the same documents might score a few cells one notch differently. Every cell carries its evidence and URL so the coding can be audited and challenged.

# How the poll-of-polls and seat forecast work

*Covers `data/forecast.json`, produced by `tools/forecast.py` from `data/polls-2026.json` (refreshed by
`tools/polls_update.py`) and `data/polls-history/*.json`. Written 23 October 2026; the numbers quoted below are from that
day's run and are superseded by whatever `data/forecast.json` currently says. Election day: Saturday 7 November 2026.*

## How to read it (plain English)

1. **Poll average** – where the public polls put each party *today*, after adjusting each pollster for its habitual lean
   and weighting recent, larger polls more. The narrow interval beside it only says how noisy the polls are.
2. **Forecast vote** – the poll average plus two extra kinds of uncertainty: how far New Zealand's final polls have missed
   the result at the last five elections, and how much support can still move before 7 November. This interval is wider,
   and it is the one that matters.
3. **Seats** – we run the real MMP rules (5% or an electorate seat; Sainte-Laguë; 120 seats plus overhang) on 40,000
   simulated election nights. "Expected seats" is the average; the 80% range is where 8 in 10 simulations land.
4. **Bloc majority** – the share of simulations in which those parties alone hold more than half of all seats
   (61 of 120, 62 of 122 or 123). It says the seats would exist, not that the parties would agree to govern.
5. **Rounding is deliberate.** Probabilities are rounded to the nearest 1% and seats to whole numbers because the inputs do
   not support anything finer. A 70% chance means the other outcome happens about 3 times in 10.

## 1. Pooling the polls

**Data.** Every public party-vote poll since the 2023 election, as tabulated on Wikipedia with fieldwork dates, sample
size and a link to the pollster's own release ([Opinion polling for the 2026 New Zealand general election][wp2026]).
`tools/polls_update.py` re-reads that article every six hours through the MediaWiki API, adds new rows, never deletes or
overwrites an existing row, tags each series (`pollster_key`) so renamed series stay together, and marks party- or
corporate-commissioned polls that are published selectively (`internal: true` – Talbot Mills, Anacta, Curia's own
releases). Pollster metadata (who commissions, who does the fieldwork, mode) is stored under `pollsters`.

**Latent trend.** Each party's support is treated as an unobserved quantity that polls measure with noise – the
"pooling the polls" framework of Jackman (2005) [[1]], used for multi-party systems by Linzer (2013) [[2]] and, for New
Zealand, by Peter Ellis's `nz-election-forecast` state-space model for 2017 and 2020 [[3]][[4]]. We use a transparent
non-Bayesian version of the same idea: at any date *t* the estimate is the weighted mean of house-adjusted polls with
fieldwork ending on or before *t*, weight

    w = 2^(−age/21 days) × √(n/1000) × (0.5 if internal)

*Half-life 21 days.* The random-walk state-space models fitted to NZ data imply latent support drifts by roughly
0.1–0.3 points a day for a major party [[3]], so a poll three weeks old carries about half the information of a new
one; with only ~4–6 public polls a month, a shorter half-life makes the average jump around on single polls and a longer
one lags real movement (compare the 2020 campaign, when National fell 5 points in six weeks). Weighting by √n is the
standard inverse-variance weight for a binomial proportion, capped by not letting one 1,700-person poll dominate.
The estimate is **one-sided** (only polls up to *t*), so the weekly trend series shows what was knowable at the time
and the backtest is honest.

**House effects.** Each pollster's house effect for each party is its mean deviation from the pooled trend over the term
(iterated five times so trend and house effects are mutually consistent), shrunk by n/(n+2) and constrained to
**sum to zero across the independent public pollsters** (1 News–Verian, RNZ–Reid Research, Taxpayers' Union–Curia,
Roy Morgan, The Post/Freshwater Strategy). Sum-to-zero is the identifying constraint Jackman used; Ellis instead
anchored house effects to past election results, which is better when pollsters are stable but is not possible for
series that did not exist in 2023 (Freshwater, Anacta). Internal polls receive a house effect but do not anchor the
average. Consequence, stated plainly in the JSON: house effects describe *relative* leans; if every pollster shares a
bias (as in 2020) the average shares it. On 23 Oct 2026 the largest estimated leans were Roy Morgan −2.1 on Labour and
+1.5 on Greens, Talbot Mills +3.0 on Labour, Freshwater and Reid Research +2 on Labour, Verian +1.2 on National.

**Undecided voters.** All NZ pollsters publish shares of decided voters (5–15% undecided excluded), so the polls already
sum to ~100 and no reallocation is done; "others" is implied. The historical calibration below measures the error that
results, so a separate undecided adjustment would double-count.

Outputs: current aggregate with 80%/95% intervals (`parties[].poll_average*`), the weekly trend from Nov 2023
(`trend_weekly`), per-pollster house effects with poll counts and the latest poll from each (`pollsters`).

## 2. Calibrating the error empirically

`tools/polls_update.py` also parses the polling articles for 2011, 2014, 2017, 2020 and 2023 into
`data/polls-history/`. For each election the final-three-weeks pooled average (√n weights, no house adjustment) is
compared with the official party vote (`data/elections/<year>.json`). Results on the 23 Oct 2026 run
(`calibration.error_table` has every row):

| Party size (final polls) | n | RMSE | mean abs error | mean bias (result − polls) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ≥20% | 10 | 3.1 | 2.5 | −0.5 |
| 5–20% | 10 | 1.2 | 0.9 | −0.4 |
| <5% | 21 | 0.8 | 0.5 | +0.3 |

Error grows with party size roughly like a binomial proportion, so the model SD is
`k·√(p(100−p))/10` with `k` fitted by least squares on squared errors (k ≈ 0.60: SD 3.0 at 45%, 2.7 at 30%,
1.8 at 10%, 1.3 at 5%, floor 0.6 for tiny parties). Squared error rather than variance is used so that historical bias
*widens* the interval instead of being used to shift the mean – we do not assume a direction. This is the approach
recommended by Shirani-Mehr, Rothschild, Goel and Gelman (2018), who find real-world poll error is about twice the
nominal sampling margin because of shared, non-sampling error [[5]]; the international average absolute error for
final-week polls is ~2 points and has not worsened over time (Jennings & Wlezien 2018, 351 elections) [[6]].

**Direction of past errors, from the data (not assumed):**

- *National* was overstated by the final polls in 2011 (−4.2), 2014 (−0.9) and 2020 (−5.6) and understated in 2017
  (+3.6) and 2023 (+2.5). Largest single-party errors on record; both directions.
- *Greens* were overstated in four of five elections (2011 −1.1, 2014 −2.0, 2017 −0.4, 2023 −1.5; 2020 +0.5).
- *NZ First* was understated in 2011 (+2.8), 2014 (+2.1) and 2020 (+0.1), overstated in 2017 (−0.2) and 2023 (−0.5)
  – so the "polls always understate Winston" rule held for the landline era but not for the last two elections.
- *Labour*: no net bias (mean −0.0) but a 3.7-point overstatement in 2017 and 3.4 understatement in 2020.
- *ACT* slightly overstated in four of five; *Te Pāti Māori* slightly understated in three of five (all < 0.7).

These findings match the 1News retrospective of final-poll accuracy 2002–2023 [[7]] and Ellis's house-effect
analyses of the 2011–2014 pollsters [[8]].

**Correlation.** Errors are correlated across parties: when National is overstated, Labour tends to be understated
(empirical r = −0.86 over five elections, shrunk to −0.54 because five observations cannot pin a correlation down;
pairs need four shared elections; the matrix is forced positive-definite). These correlations feed the multivariate
draws, so "National high and Labour low" scenarios appear at the right frequency rather than independently.

**Movement before election day.** A random-walk drift term, variance per day estimated from this term's own week-to-week
trend changes (half attributed to real movement, half to poll noise), multiplied by the days remaining – the same
random-walk assumption as Jackman and Ellis. Fifteen days out it adds ~0.5 points of SD for a major party.

Total forecast SD per party = √(calibrated error² + aggregate standard error² + drift²), shown in
`parties[].uncertainty`.

## 3. Monte Carlo seat simulation

40,000 draws (fixed seed, so reruns on unchanged data are byte-identical).

1. **Party votes** – a multivariate logit-normal around the poll average with the covariance above. The logit scale
   keeps small parties positive and gives them the right-skewed uncertainty seen historically (a 1.7% party is more
   likely to reach 3% than to fall to 0.4%).
2. **Epsom** – ACT's insurance seat. David Seymour won by 8,142 in 2023 against Paul Goldsmith (National), who stands
   again; no 2026 Epsom poll exists. P(ACT holds) = 0.90. Because ACT polls 9–11% this only matters if ACT falls below 5%.
3. **The seven Māori electorates** – these decide the overhang because Te Pāti Māori's party vote (~1.7%) is far below
   its likely electorate seats. For each seat the decided-voter candidate shares are 0.7 × the mean of the electorate
   polls from the last 45 days (Whakaata Māori–Curia, Mata–Horizon; n≈500–700, listed in
   `electorates.maori_seats[].polls_used`) + 0.3 × the same party's 2023 candidate share (new candidates get a zero
   prior; for the two MPs who have since left Te Pāti Māori, half of their 2023 vote is credited to their new vehicle –
   Mariameno Kapa-Kingi's Te Tai Tokerau Party, Tākuta Ferris as an independent). Each candidate is drawn with
   SD = √(sampling + 9²) points: Māori-roll polls are small and have missed badly before, and incumbency, turnout and the
   split on the left (Labour, Greens, TPM, TTT all competing) make these genuinely uncertain. The 2025 Tāmaki Makaurau
   by-election (Kaipara 6,948 v Henare 3,429, low turnout) is noted as context but the 2023 general-election shares are
   the prior. An independent winner is deducted from the 120 before allocation; a Te Tai Tokerau Party winner makes that
   party eligible for list seats on its (~0.3%) party vote, which yields none, so its seat becomes overhang.
4. **Allocation** – parties with ≥5% or ≥1 electorate seat share the list seats by Sainte-Laguë; each party takes the
   greater of its allocation and its electorate seats (overhang). Verified against 2023 (48/34/15/11/8/4, TPM 6 → 122).
   General electorates won by National, Labour or the Greens are assumed never to exceed their list entitlement, so they
   are not simulated. TOP has no realistic electorate (its 2023 Ilam bid is not repeated), so it lives or dies at 5%.
5. **Outputs** – expected seats and 80%/95% ranges per party, seat histograms, P(≥5%), P(wins an electorate),
   P(in Parliament), probability of a majority for National+ACT+NZ First, Labour+Green+TPM, those blocs with TOP, and
   "no bloc has a majority"; P(TOP holds the balance of power), P(NZ First holds it), P(overhang), total-seat
   distribution, and the single most frequent seat combination.

## 4. Track record (backtest)

The same aggregator – polls to 14 days before each election, house effects from that term, calibration from the *other*
four elections – versus the official result (`historical_track_record.elections`):

| Election | forecast 2 wks out → result (major parties) | biggest miss | inside 80% | inside 95% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | Nat 53.1→47.3, Lab 28.5→27.5, Grn 10.3→11.1, NZF 2.9→6.6 | NZF +3.7, Nat −5.8 (late "teapot tape" swing) | 5/8 | 5/8 |
| 2014 | Nat 48.7→47.0, Lab 25.9→25.1, Grn 12.7→10.7, NZF 5.5→8.7 | NZF +3.1 | 6/7 | 6/7 |
| 2017 | Nat 40.6→44.5, Lab 37.2→36.9, NZF 9.3→7.2, Grn 7.9→6.3 | Nat +3.8 | 6/6 | 6/6 |
| 2020 | Lab 48.8→50.0, Nat 30.4→25.6, Grn 7.5→7.9, ACT 6.7→7.6 | Nat −4.8 | 7/8 | 8/8 |
| 2023 | Nat 36.1→38.1, Lab 26.6→26.9, Grn 12.4→11.6, ACT 11.7→8.6, NZF 5.3→6.1 | ACT −3.1 | 6/7 | 7/7 |
| **All** | | | **30/36 (83%)** | **32/36 (89%)** |

Coverage of 83% for nominal 80% intervals is on target; the 95% intervals are a little narrow (89%), driven by the 2011
NZ First surge and Conservative Party entry that no two-weeks-out poll average could see. The largest party was correctly
identified every time; the 2017 and 2020 National misses show the common NZ pattern of the incumbent-side vote being
mis-measured late.

**Incumbent governments, mid-term poll to polling day** (`incumbent_*` fields): National 2011 50.7 → 47.3 (−3.4);
National 2014 46.3 → 47.0 (+0.8); National 2017 46.8 → 44.5 (−2.4); Labour 2020 48.2 → 50.0 (+1.8, COVID);
Labour 2023 36.0 → 26.9 (−9.1). For 2026, National stood at 33.3 in May 2025 (18 months out) and 28.6 in the
23 Oct 2026 average – already an unusually large fall for a first-term government.

## 5. Caveats (read these)

- **Polling error is the dominant uncertainty.** The final polls missed a major party by 4–6 points in 2011 and 2020.
  Our intervals include those misses, but a miss bigger than anything since 2011 is always possible.
- **Threshold cliffs.** TOP (~6%) and, to a lesser degree, NZ First sit near 5%. A one-point move can shift 6–10 seats
  between blocs, so bloc probabilities are far less certain than vote shares look.
- **Electorate assumptions** (Epsom, Māori seats) rest on a handful of small polls and stated judgements; they are the
  weakest input and are published in full so you can disagree with them.
- **Late swing and undecideds.** About a fifth of voters decide in the final fortnight; advance voting (from 26 Oct)
  blunts this only partly. Polls exclude 5–15% undecided.
- **Shared bias.** House effects are relative; a bias common to all pollsters is invisible until election night.
- **Selective publication.** Internal/corporate polls (Talbot Mills, Anacta, Curia) appear when someone chooses to
  release them; they are down-weighted but still present.
- **No coalition model.** Majority = seats exist, not that a government forms. Post-election bargaining (NZ First, TOP)
  is outside the model.
- **Only seven parties.** A minor party winning an electorate or crossing 5% from nowhere is not simulated.

## 6. Reproducing it

    python3 tools/polls_update.py          # refresh polls (needs network; --offline re-parses the cache)
    python3 tools/forecast.py              # writes data/forecast.json (≈3 s)
    python3 tools/forecast.py --asof 2026-09-01 --out /tmp/f.json   # what it would have said on an earlier date

`.github/workflows/polls.yml` does this every six hours and commits the result (requires GitHub Actions enabled).

# How to vote in the 2026 General Election

*Election day is **Saturday 7 November 2026**, 9am to 7pm. Enrolment closed at **midnight Sunday 25 October**. Last checked against the Electoral Commission's pages on Fri 23 Oct 2026.*

> **The rules changed this year.** In December 2025 Parliament passed the Electoral Amendment Act 2025, which (Public Act 2025 No 82, Royal assent 19 December 2025, most of it in force from 20 December 2025). It closes enrolment 13 days before election day, so there is no enrolling at a voting place during advance voting or on election day; sets a 12-day advance voting period; and bars more sentenced prisoners from voting. Sources: Ministry of Justice summary (justice.govt.nz, retrieved 23 Oct 2026); RNZ, 'Electoral Amendment Bill passes its third reading in Parliament' (Dec 2025); Electoral Act 1993 as at 1 January 2026, s 3(1) 'close of registration', s 80, s 171B.

This page is generated from [`data/guide/howtovote.json`](../data/guide/howtovote.json). Every fact links to the Electoral Commission page (vote.nz / elections.nz), the Act, or the news report it came from. Where we could not verify something, we say so at the bottom. It is not legal advice. If your situation is unusual, call the Commission on **0800 36 76 56** (free, 24/7).

## First-time voter checklist

| # | Step | You are done when... | Link |
|---|------|----------------------|------|
| 1 | **Check you are eligible** | You are 18 or older on election day, a NZ citizen or a resident for electoral purposes (your visa doesn't make you leave by a set date), and you have lived in NZ continuously for 12 months or more at some time in your life. If you are 17 now but turn 18 by 7 November, you can enrol. | [link](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote) |
| 2 | **Check you are enrolled at your current address, before midnight Sunday 25 October** | The online check at vote.nz shows your name and current address (you need a NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe), or you have called 0800 36 76 56 and been told you are enrolled. After midnight 25 October nothing can be changed and you cannot enrol at a voting place. | [link](https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/enrol-or-update-online) |
| 3 | **Pick where and when you will vote** | You have looked up a voting place and its hours on the official map (hours vary before election day), or you know a place that is open 9am to 7pm on Saturday 7 November. You can vote at any voting place in NZ, but it is quicker close to home. | [link](https://map.vote.nz) |
| 4 | **Know what to bring: nothing is required** | You know no ID is needed. If you have an EasyVote card (sent to everyone enrolled by 4 October, by email or post) bring it on paper, on your phone or as a screenshot; it makes finding you on the roll faster. | [link](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/communications-from-the-electoral-commission/your-easyvote-card) |
| 5 | **Understand the two ticks** | You know you make one tick on the left for a party (party vote) and one tick on the right for a local candidate (electorate vote). One tick for each. You may do just one side if you want. If you make a mistake, ask for a new paper. | [link](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-do) |
| 6 | **Plan ahead if you will be away or overseas** | Away from home in NZ: you know you can vote at any voting place (you will fill in a short special-vote declaration). Overseas on or after 21 October: you know you must be enrolled by 25 October, then download your papers at vote.nz/overseas, sign the declaration with a witness, and upload by 7pm NZ time on 7 November. | [link](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/vote-from-overseas) |
| 7 | **Get help if you need it** | You know a friend, family member or voting place worker can go behind the screen with you, read the paper and mark it as you ask (they can't tell you who to vote for). If you are blind, have low vision or a physical disability, you have registered for telephone dictation voting (0800 028 028) by noon on 7 November. If you can't get to a voting place, you have called 0800 36 76 56 or your electorate manager. | [link](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote) |

| Sun 4 Oct 2026 | Writ Day. If you were enrolled by this date you get an EasyVote card and are on the printed roll. Anyone who enrols or updates after this date casts a special vote. | [source](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/key-dates) |

## 1. Am I allowed to vote?

*For: everyone; first-time voters; new residents; people on visas; people in prison or on remand.*

- You can enrol and vote if all three are true: you are 18 or older; you are a New Zealand citizen or a 'resident for electoral purposes'; and you have lived in New Zealand continuously for 12 months or more at some time in your life. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote) <sub>vote.nz, 'Are you eligible to enrol and vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act 1993 s 74</sub>
- 'Resident for electoral purposes' means you live in New Zealand lawfully and your visa does not make you leave by a set date. Resident-visa holders (including the 2021 Resident Visa) qualify. People on work, student or visitor visas with an end date do not. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- If you are 17 you can fill in the form now. You are enrolled automatically on your 18th birthday. If you turn 18 on or before 7 November 2026, you can vote, as long as you applied to enrol by midnight 25 October. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/communications-from-the-electoral-commission/your-easyvote-card) <sub>vote.nz EasyVote page and eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- If you live in New Zealand and are eligible, enrolling is compulsory by law. Voting itself is not compulsory. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote) <sub>vote.nz, 'Need help to vote?' (dementia section) and 'Facts about New Zealand elections', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Prison (changed in 2025): you cannot vote if you are serving a sentence of 3 years or more. You also cannot vote if you are serving a sentence of less than 3 years for any offence committed on or after 20 December 2025. You CAN still vote if you are serving less than 3 years and all your offences happened before 20 December 2025, or if you are on remand, home detention or a community sentence. The Commission works with Corrections to provide voting for eligible prisoners. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote) <sub>vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act 1993 s 80(1)(d) as at 1 Jan 2026 (raw/howtovote/electoral-act-1993-2026-01-01.pdf); Ministry of Justice, 'Electoral law changes'</sub>
- You also cannot vote if you are a NZ citizen who has not been in New Zealand in the last 3 years, a resident (non-citizen) who has not been in NZ in the last 12 months, if you have been held in a psychiatric hospital for more than 3 years after a criminal charge, or if you are on the Corrupt Practices List. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote) <sub>vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 80</sub>
- Homeless? You can enrol at the address where you spend most of your time, or the last address where you lived for a month or more. You need a postal address (a PO Box or a friend, family member, church or support group who will hold mail for you). [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/are-you-eligible-to-enrol-and-vote) <sub>vote.nz eligibility page, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>

**Notes**

- The brief said 'prisoners now barred under the 2025 Act'. Verified with a correction: the ban is not total. Sentenced prisoners serving under 3 years can still vote if all their offences were before 20 December 2025 (Electoral Act s 80(1)(d)(i)-(ii); vote.nz). RNZ (Dec 2025) reported the Act 'bans prisoners from voting'; 1News (16 Oct 2026) called it 'a total ban on prisoner voting for prisoners sentenced after December 2025'. The Act's wording turns on when the offence happened, not the sentencing date.
- Unsure? Call 0800 36 76 56. The law is Electoral Act 1993 ss 74 and 80.

## 2. Enrol or update your details by midnight, Sunday 25 October

*For: everyone who has moved house; first-time voters; people on the unpublished roll; Māori choosing a roll.*

- Deadline: midnight, Sunday 25 October 2026. The law now closes the roll 13 days before election day. You cannot enrol or change your address after this, and you cannot enrol at a voting place during advance voting or on election day. Voting place staff can't make exceptions; the rule is set by law. *(Sun 25 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-do) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do' and eligibility pages, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 3(1) 'close of registration' (inserted by Electoral Amendment Act 2025 s 4(2)); 1News 16 Oct 2026 ('there are no exceptions, the Electoral Commission says')</sub>
- Fastest way: online at vote.nz with your NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe verified identity. The same page lets you check what address you are enrolled at. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/enrol-or-update-online) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Commission release 22 Oct 2026</sub>
- No ID? Fill in the form online and have it emailed or posted to you to sign ('Enrol without ID' / 'Update without ID'), download the PDF form, call 0800 36 76 56, or text your name and address to 3676. Then return the signed form by upload (vote.nz/upload), email (enrol@vote.nz), or drop it at an enrolment hub. Hub times and places are at vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/enrolment-in-your-community. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/other-ways-to-enrol) <sub>vote.nz 'Other ways to enrol', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Post is slow: the Commission recommended posting forms by Tuesday 20 October. It will accept forms that arrive by post on Tuesday 27 October but not after. If you still have a paper form, upload or email it, or take it to a hub. *(Tue 20 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/other-ways-to-enrol) <sub>vote.nz 'Other ways to enrol', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Moved house but still enrolled at an old address? You can still vote, but you may need to cast a special vote. If your new home is in a different electorate, only your party vote will count. Update your address by 25 October so both votes count. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/enrol-by-25-october) <sub>vote.nz 'Enrol by 25 October', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Dormant roll: if mail from the Commission came back from your old address you may be on the 'dormant roll'. You can still vote (as a special vote) but, again, if you have moved electorate only your party vote counts. Updating your address before 25 October fixes this. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/enrol-by-25-october) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Not enrolled at any address by midnight 25 October? The Commission says you will not be able to vote in this election. If you turn up believing you are enrolled, you can cast a special vote, but it will be disallowed if you turn out not to be enrolled. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/enrol-by-25-october) <sub>vote.nz 'Enrol by 25 October', retrieved 2026-10-23; 1News 16 Oct 2026</sub>
- Unpublished roll: if you fear for your safety, you can ask to go on the confidential unpublished roll (download the form or call 0800 36 76 56). Your details are kept off printed rolls. You will then cast a special vote, you can't check or update your details online, and you can't download overseas voting papers. [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/can-you-go-on-the-unpublished-roll) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Māori roll or general roll: if you are of Māori descent you choose a roll when you first enrol. You vote for the same parties on either roll; the difference is which electorate candidates you choose from. Already-enrolled Māori could change rolls until midnight 6 August 2026; the 3-month pre-election freeze now applies. If you are enrolling for the first time you can still choose either roll up to 25 October. *(Thu 6 Aug 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/maori-enrolment/about-the-option/about/maori-roll-or-general-roll) <sub>vote.nz key dates and 'Māori roll or general roll?'; Electoral Commission release '17,000 Māori voters change rolls', 18 Aug 2026</sub>

**Notes**

- Why it changed: the Government said late enrolments put 'too much strain on the system' and slowed the count (Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith, quoted by RNZ, July 2025). The Attorney-General reported the cut-off 'appears to constitute an unjustified limit' on the right to vote under the Bill of Rights Act (reported by RNZ). The Chief Electoral Officer told MPs the change was 'not a change that we recommended' and would not make official results faster than 20 days (RNZ, Sept 2025). Labour has said it would reverse the change (RNZ). Both sides' views are reported here; the guide takes no position.
- Scale: in 2023, about 450,000 people enrolled or updated in the final two weeks, including about 110,000 on election day (1News, 16 Oct 2026, citing Commission data). The Commission expects about 55,000 special votes to be disallowed this year, five times more than usual, because the voter turns out not to be enrolled (1News).
- On 21 October 2026, 3,729,667 people were enrolled, 92.1% of those eligible; only 68.6% of 18 to 24 year olds were enrolled (Electoral Commission, 22 Oct 2026).
- Enrolment packs were posted 17 to 22 August 2026; if you didn't get one, your address was out of date or you were not enrolled (Electoral Commission, 10 Aug 2026). The Commission also used data matching with NZTA and Internal Affairs to contact 170,000 people in September (release 17 Sep 2026).

## 3. When and where to vote

*For: everyone; shift workers; people voting away from home.*

- Advance voting: Monday 26 October to Friday 6 November. You can vote at any voting place in New Zealand. Days and hours differ from place to place, and some places open only before election day or only on election day, so check before you go. *(Mon 26 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/find-a-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz 'Find a voting place', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 171B (12-day advance period)</sub>
- Election day: Saturday 7 November, every voting place open 9am to 7pm. If you are inside a voting place at 7pm waiting to vote, you can still vote. *(Sat 7 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/key-dates) <sub>vote.nz key dates; Electoral Act s 161</sub>
- Find a place: use the official map at map.vote.nz (search your address; filter by day, 'open now', accessibility, Whare Pōti Māori, reo rua), the list by electorate and suburb on vote.nz, posters at your local supermarket or library, or call 0800 36 76 56. [[source]](https://map.vote.nz) <sub>vote.nz 'Find a voting place'; Electoral Commission releases 7 and 22 Oct 2026</sub>
- Vote close to home if you can. It is faster because your name is on the printed roll there. Anywhere else you can still vote, but you fill in a special-vote declaration first. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-do) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- What to bring: nothing. No ID is needed. Bring your EasyVote card if you have one (paper, phone or screenshot); it helps staff find you on the roll. You can vote without it. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/facts-about-new-zealand-elections) <sub>vote.nz 'Facts about New Zealand elections' ('No ID is required') and EasyVote page, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- EasyVote cards went to everyone enrolled by 4 October, by email (from no-reply@easy.vote.nz; follow-up texts from 5101) or by post, between 14 and 22 October. Check your spam folder. If you enrolled after 4 October you won't get one, but you can still vote. [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/easyvote-cards-are-on-their-way) <sub>Electoral Commission release, 14 Oct 2026; vote.nz EasyVote page</sub>
- Quieter times: if you prefer less crowding or need assistance, the Commission says 9am to 11am and 2pm to 4pm on weekdays are usually best. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote) <sub>vote.nz 'Need help to vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Time off work on election day: if you haven't had a reasonable chance to vote before starting work, your employer must let you leave by 3pm for the rest of the day, with no pay docked. If you do essential work after 3pm, you get a reasonable time off earlier in the day, with up to 2 hours paid. Employers who refuse can be fined up to $1,000. *(Sat 7 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place) <sub>Electoral Act 1993 s 162 (verified in the consolidated Act as at 1 Jan 2026, raw/howtovote/electoral-act-1993-2026-01-01.pdf); vote.nz 'Can't get to a voting place?' (time away from work section)</sub>

**Notes**

- Staff wear orange vests and will guide you. Many are working their first election; the Commission asks for patience if there are delays (vote.nz, 'What to expect at the voting place').
- Monday 26 October is Labour Day; 207 voting places open that day (Commission release 22 Oct 2026; RNZ explainer 23 Oct 2026).
