## 4. Voting away from home, special votes, and voting when you can't get to a voting place

*For: students and workers away from home; people who enrolled after 4 October; people on the unpublished or dormant roll; people in hospital, care homes or prison; people with illness or mobility problems.*

- A special vote is a normal vote plus a short declaration form you sign. You cast one if your name is not on the printed roll where you vote: because you enrolled or updated after Writ Day (4 October), you are voting outside your electorate, you are on the unpublished roll, you are on the dormant roll, or you are voting from overseas or away from a voting place. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-do) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do'; elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'; Electoral Act s 61</sub>
- Voting in another electorate: you get the ballot paper for YOUR home electorate, so your electorate vote still counts, as long as you are enrolled there. If you vote for an electorate you are not enrolled in, the electorate vote is disallowed and only your party vote is counted ('Party Vote Only'). [[source]](https://elections.nz/democracy-in-nz/about-elections/how-are-general-election-votes-counted/) <sub>elections.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- How special votes are counted: they are sent back to your home electorate, every declaration is checked against the roll, and they are added to the official count. They can arrive up to 10 days after election day. That is why they are not in election-night results and why official results take until 27 November. *(Fri 27 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://elections.nz/democracy-in-nz/about-elections/how-are-general-election-votes-counted/) <sub>elections.nz; vote.nz 'What happens after an election?'</sub>
- Can't get to a voting place (illness, mobility)? Someone can collect your voting papers for you ('takeaway' voting). Sign a written authorisation (form on vote.nz, or handwritten with your name, phone, enrolled address, which roll you are on, and a line authorising the bearer). They bring the papers to you; you complete them with a witnessed special-vote declaration; they must be back at a voting place before 7pm on 7 November. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz 'Can't get to a voting place?', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Nobody to collect them? Contact your electorate manager (list on vote.nz). It may be possible for papers to be delivered to you and collected again. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/contact-your-electorate-manager) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- In hospital: a friend or family member can bring you your voting papers. If you know you will be in hospital, the Commission suggests voting in advance. In a care home or rest home: you don't need to do anything; the electorate manager arranges voting with your home's manager. Ask your home what has been arranged. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Blind, low vision or a physical disability that stops you marking the paper: use telephone dictation voting (see Accessibility section). Remote locations (DOC islands, offshore installations, vessels in NZ waters): apply early to remote@vote.nz. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place/remote-voting) <sub>vote.nz 'Remote voting', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- In prison or on remand and eligible? The Commission works with Corrections to provide voting services. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>

**Notes**

- The Commission forecast around 700,000 special votes for 2026 (Chief Electoral Officer to the Justice Committee, RNZ, Sept 2025). In 2023 there were 603,257 special votes, 20.9% of all votes (Commission, 3 Nov 2023).
- 'Voting from home' in the sense of postal voting for everyone does not exist for general elections in New Zealand; the options above (collected papers, electorate-manager delivery, dictation, remote and overseas services) are what the Commission offers.

## 5. Voting from overseas

*For: New Zealanders living abroad; travellers; students overseas; Defence Force and public servants posted overseas.*

- Who can: you must be enrolled, 18+, have lived in NZ for 12+ continuous months at some time, and be either a NZ citizen who has been in NZ within the last 3 years, or a resident for electoral purposes who has been in NZ within the last 12 months. Public servants, diplomats and Defence Force members posted overseas, and their families, qualify however long they have been away. Enrolling from overseas is optional. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/vote-from-overseas) <sub>vote.nz 'How to vote from overseas', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 80(1)(a)-(b)</sub>
- Enrol or update by midnight Sunday 25 October, NZ time. You can't download papers until your enrolment is processed, so do it early. Your electorate is where you last lived for a month or more. If you have been away too long to update online, email overseas@vote.nz. *(Sun 25 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/enrolling/get-ready-to-enrol/enrol-from-overseas) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Voting opened Wednesday 21 October (NZ time). The easiest way: download your papers at vote.nz/overseas (a 3-page PDF: instructions, declaration, ballot paper), mark them on screen or print and mark by hand, then upload them. You must be physically outside New Zealand when you download; if you download while still in NZ your vote will not be counted. *(Wed 21 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/downloading-your-voting-papers) <sub>vote.nz 'Downloading your voting papers' and 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- The declaration must be signed by you AND a witness who is physically with you. Typed signatures and handwriting-style fonts are not accepted; draw or insert an image of your real signature. Tick your reason for a special vote (e.g. outside NZ on election day). Your witness can be a relative, flatmate, colleague or associate, any registered NZ elector, or an official such as a notary. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/how-to-complete-your-voting-papers) <sub>vote.nz 'How to complete your voting papers' and 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Upload at uvp.elections.govt.nz by 7pm on Saturday 7 November, NZ time. Late papers cannot be accepted. Upload once only: more than one submission may mean your vote doesn't count. Files: JPG, PNG, GIF, PDF or TIFF, 10 KB to 10 MB, whole page visible including the 7-digit number top right. *(Sat 7 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/uploading-your-voting-papers) <sub>vote.nz 'Uploading your voting papers', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- In person: 64 overseas locations offer in-person or postal voting, including 10 in Australia. Hours and closing dates differ, some are appointment-only or postal-only, most are closed at weekends, and ALL overseas voting places are closed on election day, 7 November. Check the lookup before you go. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/find-an-overseas-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz 'Find an overseas voting place'; Electoral Commission release 21 Oct 2026</sub>
- On the unpublished roll? You can't download papers. Ask your nearest overseas voting place for a postal vote or collect papers in person, or email overseas@vote.nz. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/common-questions) <sub>vote.nz 'Common questions', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Help: overseas@vote.nz or +64 9 909 4182. Blind or disabled voters overseas can use telephone dictation voting on +64 4 471 2000 (register first). [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/overseas/common-questions) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>

**Notes**

- In 2023, 88% of overseas voters used the download service; 77,295 overseas votes were received (62,787 in 2020). About 126,000 enrolled voters have told the Commission they live overseas, 64% of them in Australia (Electoral Commission, 21 Oct 2026).
- Niueans, Tokelauans and Cook Islanders vote on the citizen rule (in NZ within 3 years); Australians on the resident rule (within 12 months) (vote.nz 'How to vote from overseas').
- The brief's 'from 21 Oct?' is confirmed: overseas voting started Wednesday 21 October 2026 (vote.nz key dates; Commission release 21 Oct 2026).

## 6. Help to vote and accessible voting

*For: blind and low-vision voters; Deaf voters; disabled voters; people with dementia or cognitive impairment; anyone who needs a hand.*

- A support person: a friend, family member or voting place worker can go behind the screen with you, read out the paper, and mark it as you ask. They cannot tell you who to vote for. The choice must be yours and you must be present. Nobody can vote for you, not even with power of attorney. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote) <sub>vote.nz 'Need help to vote?', retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Act s 170</sub>
- Telephone dictation voting is for people who are blind, partially blind or have a physical disability that stops them marking the paper. You must register every election, even if you used it before. Register from Monday 5 October to noon on Saturday 7 November by calling 0800 028 028 (option 1) or +64 4 471 2000 from overseas. Registration hours: weekdays 9am to 7pm; from 26 October also Saturdays 9am to 3pm; election day 9am to noon. *(Mon 5 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place/telephone-dictation-voting) <sub>vote.nz 'Telephone dictation voting', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Then vote by phone from Wednesday 21 October to 7pm on Saturday 7 November (0800 028 028, option 2). You give your registration number and the answer to a secret question, not your name. One official reads out the candidates and parties and marks your paper; a second official checks it back with you. Dictation voting hours: weekdays 9am to 7pm, Saturdays 9am to 3pm (from 26 Oct), election day 9am to 7pm. *(Wed 21 Oct 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/cant-get-to-a-voting-place/telephone-dictation-voting) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23; Electoral Commission release 21 Oct 2026</sub>
- Accessible voting places: 1,679 are fully accessible; NZSL interpreters are at six locations; three places have quiet times. The map at map.vote.nz can be filtered by accessibility. [[source]](https://map.vote.nz) <sub>Electoral Commission release 7 Oct 2026; vote.nz 'Find a voting place'</sub>
- Information in other formats: audio, Braille, large print, Easy Read and New Zealand Sign Language (NZSL) versions of the enrolling and voting guides are at vote.nz. Easy Read: 'Get ready to enrol and vote in the 2026 General Election' (PDF). Most vote.nz pages also have te reo Māori and NZSL versions (language toggle at the top). [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/resources/information-in-accessible-formats) <sub>vote.nz 'Information in accessible formats' and 'Information in Easy Read', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Access 2026 is the Commission's accessibility action plan: 20 accessible services for Deaf and disabled people, tāngata Turi (Deaf Māori) and tāngata whaikaha Māori (disabled Māori), with Easy Read, large print, audio and Braille summaries. [[source]](https://elections.nz/about/about-the-electoral-commission/corporate-publications/access-2026-action-plan) <sub>Electoral Commission release 7 Sep 2026; elections.nz Access 2026 page, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Dementia or cognitive impairment: there is no capacity test for voting. A person can vote if they want to and can clearly show their choice at the time; a support person must follow their instructions. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/need-help-to-vote) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Te reo Māori: 67 bilingual (reo rua) voting places let you vote in te reo Māori or English; more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori places are at marae, kura, wānanga and community spaces. Filter the map for 'Whare Pōti Māori' and 'Reo rua'. [[source]](https://map.vote.nz) <sub>Electoral Commission release 7 Oct 2026</sub>

**Notes**

- Quiet times at voting places are generally 9am to 11am and 2pm to 4pm on weekdays (vote.nz).
- The Access 2026 'Quick guide to accessible voting services' PDF could not be downloaded (bot protection); its contents are summarised from the Access 2026 web page and the telephone dictation page instead.
- Disabled voters told 1News (5 Oct 2026, cited in docs/FEATURE_REVIEW.md) they were still hunting for accessible booths; the map's accessibility filter and 0800 36 76 56 are the Commission's answers.

## 7. First time voting? What happens inside, and the two ticks

*For: first-time voters; students; anyone who wants a refresher.*

- Arrive. Staff in orange vests greet you. Give your EasyVote card, or your name and address, to the person issuing papers. They find you on the roll (electronic roll for dormant-roll voters) and hand you your voting paper. If you are not on the printed roll you fill in a special-vote declaration first. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-expect-at-the-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz 'What to expect' and 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Go to a voting screen and vote in private, with a pen. You get two votes on one paper. LEFT side: your party vote. Tick ONE circle next to the party you want in government. RIGHT side: your electorate vote. Tick ONE circle next to the candidate you want as the MP for your area. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-do) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- You can tick both sides, or just one side. Both are valid. The party vote decides how many seats each party gets in Parliament; the electorate vote picks your local MP. Your EasyVote card comes with the list of candidates for your electorate; party lists are on vote.nz. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/party-lists) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do' ('vote for only one or the other, it's your choice'); elections.nz 'What happens in a general election?'</sub>
- Made a mistake? Take the 'spoilt' paper back and ask for a new one. Spoilt papers are not counted. An 'informal' vote is one where the counters cannot tell what you intended; it is recorded but does not count. If your intention is clear, your vote counts even if the paper has been drawn on. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/facts-about-new-zealand-elections) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do' (spoilt papers) and 'Facts about New Zealand elections' (informal votes), retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Fold the paper in half and put it in the ballot box. Then leave; the Commission asks voters not to linger so others feel comfortable. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-do) <sub>vote.nz 'What to do' and 'What to expect', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Phones and selfies: don't film or photograph inside a voting place. Publishing a photo or video of someone filling in their paper is a potential offence. Candidates who want to be filmed voting must arrange it in advance (returns@elections.govt.nz / the Returning Officer). [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/what-to-expect-at-the-voting-place) <sub>vote.nz 'What to expect'; Electoral Commission, 'Rules once voting starts and on election day' (PDF, 2026)</sub>
- Campaigning near voting places: during advance voting, no campaigning, election advertising or influencing voters inside a voting place or within 10 metres of its entrance. On election day those rules apply everywhere until 7pm: no campaign material (a lapel badge or rosette is allowed), no processions, no polling voters. New in 2026: nobody may give out free food, drink (except water) or entertainment within 100 metres of a voting place entrance while voting is open, unless it is their normal business. [[source]](https://elections.nz/assets/2026-General-Election/2026-Rules-once-voting-starts.pdf) <sub>Electoral Commission, 'Rules once voting starts and on election day' (raw/howtovote/rules-once-voting-starts.pdf); Ministry of Justice summary of the 2025 Act</sub>
- Social media on election day: from midnight before election day until 7pm on 7 November, you must not post or share anything likely to influence someone's party or candidate vote. There is no exemption for personal opinions online on election day. Posts made before election day can stay up if not updated. Paid election advertising online is banned on election day. *(Sat 7 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://elections.nz/guidance-and-rules/advertising-and-campaigning/social-media) <sub>elections.nz 'Social media' and vote.nz 'What to expect', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Scrutineers: you may see people with party rosettes sitting along one side. They are appointed by candidates and parties to watch, not Commission staff, and they cannot talk to voters. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/facts-about-new-zealand-elections) <sub>vote.nz 'Facts about New Zealand elections', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>

**Notes**

- Votes are counted by hand; New Zealand does not use voting machines (vote.nz, 'Facts about New Zealand elections').
- Who to vote for is your decision. This guide does not recommend anyone. RNZ's 23 Oct 2026 explainer points first-time voters to non-partisan candidate information at policy.nz and the parties' own websites.
- If you vote for an electorate you are not enrolled in (e.g. you moved and didn't update), only your party vote counts (elections.nz, 'Party Vote Only'). In 2023 more than 42,000 electorate votes were disallowed for this reason; the Commission estimated more than 72,000 could be this year (1News, 16 Oct 2026).

## 8. After you vote: results and forming a government

*For: everyone; election-night watchers.*

- Election night: advance votes are counted from 9am on election day at electorate headquarters; election-day votes are counted at each voting place after 7pm. Preliminary results go up progressively from 7pm on electionresults.govt.nz. The Commission's targets: 50% of results by 10pm and 95% by 11.30pm. *(Sat 7 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://electionresults.govt.nz) <sub>elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'; vote.nz 'What happens after an election?', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Election-night results are NOT final. They leave out all special votes (including overseas votes) and the rolls have not yet been checked. The Commission says they 'are likely to change'. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/what-happens-after-the-election) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Special votes have changed results before. 2023: after specials, National went from 50 seats to 48, Te Pāti Māori from 4 to 6, the Greens from 14 to 15; Nelson, Te Atatū, Tāmaki Makaurau (by 4 votes) and Te Tai Tokerau changed hands; National and ACT alone no longer had a majority. 603,257 special votes were 20.9% of the total. [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/official-results-for-the-2023-general-election/) <sub>Electoral Commission, 'Official results for the 2023 General Election', 3 Nov 2023</sub>
- 2020: National fell from 35 seats to 33, Labour rose from 64 to 65 and the Māori Party from 1 to 2; Maungakiekie, Northland and Whangārei switched from National to Labour. 504,625 special votes were 17% of the total. [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2020/2020-general-election-official-results/) <sub>Electoral Commission, '2020 General Election official results', 6 Nov 2020</sub>
- Official results: Friday 27 November 2026 (20 days after election day). Every vote is recounted by hand, special votes (which can arrive up to 10 days after election day) are checked and counted, and the rolls are checked for double voting. Results are published in the NZ Gazette and on electionresults.govt.nz. *(Fri 27 Nov 2026)* [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/key-dates) <sub>vote.nz key dates; elections.nz 'How are general election votes counted?'</sub>
- Recounts and challenges: a candidate or party can apply for a recount within 3 working days of the official results; an election petition to the High Court must be filed within 28 days. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/what-happens-after-the-election) <sub>vote.nz 'What happens after an election?', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Forming a government: every electorate winner gets a seat; the rest are filled from party lists in proportion to the party vote. Under MMP one party rarely wins alone, so parties negotiate a coalition or support ('confidence and supply') deal. There is no deadline for this. The outgoing government stays on as a caretaker, avoiding major decisions, until a new one is sworn in. [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/what-happens-after-the-election) <sub>vote.nz 'What happens after an election?' (Government formation); RNZ The House, 2026</sub>
- The writ is returned by 3 December 2026 with the names of elected MPs; the new Parliament's three-year term runs from that day. Parliament must meet within 6 weeks of that date (Constitution Act 1986 s 19), so by 14 January 2027 even if coalition talks are still going. The first sitting day MPs are sworn in and elect a Speaker (Commission Opening); the next day the Governor-General gives the Speech from the Throne (State Opening). *(Thu 3 Dec 2026)* [[source]](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/590326/the-house-what-to-expect-when-you-re-expecting-an-election) <sub>RNZ The House (Clerk of the House David Wilson), 2026; Constitution Act 1986 ss 17 and 19 (raw/howtovote/constitution-act-1986.pdf); vote.nz key dates</sub>

**Notes**

- Why specials lean a certain way is analysis, not Commission fact: 1News (3 Nov 2023) wrote that special votes 'have historically tended to skew left'. The guide reports the shifts, not the reasons.
- In 2023 the official count took three weeks; the Chief Electoral Officer told MPs in September 2025 the 2025 law change would not make the 20-day official result faster, because people enrolling between Writ Day and the 13-day close still cast special votes (RNZ).
- Voting papers are kept sealed for six months in case of a legal challenge, then destroyed (vote.nz).
- Parliament's and DPMC's own post-election pages (election-2026-timeline, Cabinet Office circular CO (26) 5) could not be fetched (bot protection), so government-formation steps are sourced to vote.nz, RNZ's The House and the Constitution Act.

## 9. Check before you share: official sources and where to report

*For: everyone; people who see election claims on social media.*

- The Electoral Commission's campaign, launched 29 July 2026, asks people to 'take a moment' before sharing information about enrolling and voting: 'slow down and check the information you see or hear. If you see something that doesn't look right on your social media feed, don't share it.' Waatea News reported it under the headline 'Think Before You Share'. *(Wed 29 Jul 2026)* [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/take-a-moment-before-you-share-information) <sub>Electoral Commission release, 29 Jul 2026; vote.nz 'Free and fair elections'; Waatea News, 30 Jul 2026</sub>
- Official sources for when, where and how to vote: vote.nz and 0800 36 76 56. For results: electionresults.govt.nz. The Commission's 'Facts about New Zealand elections' page answers common myths (no ID needed, no voting machines, hand counts, how specials work). [[source]](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/about/overview/free-and-fair-elections/facts-about-new-zealand-elections) <sub>vote.nz, retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Don't share misinformation even to correct it; post the correct information instead. Check that a claim really comes from a candidate's or party's real account or website. Election ads must carry a promoter statement (name and address); unpaid posts must show it on the account's About or Profile page. [[source]](https://elections.nz/guidance-and-rules/advertising-and-campaigning/social-media) <sub>elections.nz 'Social media', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>
- Where to report: misleading information about when, where or how to vote, or an ad with no promoter statement, to the Electoral Commission (elections.nz/contact, enquiries@elections.govt.nz, 0800 36 76 56). Paid or boosted social media ads: Advertising Standards Authority (asa.co.nz). TV and radio: Broadcasting Standards Authority. News content: the publisher, then the Media Council. Posts that break platform rules: report to the platform. The Commission refers suspected offences to Police; it does not regulate the content of political ads. [[source]](https://elections.nz/guidance-and-rules/advertising-and-campaigning/advice-and-complaints) <sub>elections.nz 'Advice and complaints' and 'Social media', retrieved 2026-10-23</sub>

**Notes**

- The Commission's own name for the campaign is not stated beyond the release title 'Take a moment before you share information'; 'Think before you share' is the media's phrasing (Waatea News). Not verified as an official slogan.
- The Commission has referred several 2026 election advertising matters to Police (releases 16 and 23 Oct 2026); it names the rule breached, not the content.

</details>

## Finding your nearest voting place

- **Official finder (map):** <https://map.vote.nz>  
- **List by electorate and suburb:** <https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/find-a-voting-place>  
- **Phone:** 0800 36 76 56

The official finder (map.vote.nz, redirects to map.vote.nz/voting-places) is a client-side map. It loads the whole 2026 voting-place dataset into the browser and filters it there, with an address search box (Mapbox geocoding) and filters for day, 'open now', accessibility, Whare Pōti Māori and reo rua. It takes no documented URL parameters: on 23 Oct 2026 we tested https://map.vote.nz/voting-places?electorate=Wellington%20Central and the page loaded the default view. The vote.nz list page lets you pick an electorate and suburb from drop-downs, also client-side. So the app should deep-link to https://map.vote.nz and let the voter type their address, or call 0800 36 76 56. Posters listing nearby voting places are also displayed at local supermarkets and community libraries during advance voting.

- More than 2,300 voting places open on election day (the finder data held 2,314 on 23 Oct); 207 open on Monday 26 October (finder data: 209) offering 1,437 hours of voting; the number grows towards election day. [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/voting-places-announced-for-2026-election) [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/voting-starts-on-monday)
- 1,679 fully accessible voting places; NZ Sign Language interpreters at six locations; three voting places with quiet times; more than 220 Whare Pōti Māori voting places (marae, kura, wānanga and community spaces), including 67 bilingual (reo rua) places where you can vote in te reo Māori or English. [[source]](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2026/voting-places-announced-for-2026-election)
- Votes will be taken at 2,638 locations across the whole voting period (RNZ, citing the Commission). [[source]](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1781478/where-you-can-vote-in-advance-and-on-election-day)

**Data and licence.** https://map.vote.nz/assets/map-data/locations-<hash>.json (the hash changes when the data is updated; on 23 Oct 2026 it was a 1.05 MB JSON file with 2,641 locations, each with name, address, suburb, WGS84 coordinates, accessibility code (none/partial/full), Whare Pōti Māori and reo rua flags, per-day opening hours, and the electorates it serves as a 'Home' or 'Shared' place). It is served from behind the Commission's bot protection (Incapsula) and is not published on data.govt.nz. No licence statement was found on the data file, on map.vote.nz, or on vote.nz/elections.nz (their footers say only 'Copyright © Electoral Commission New Zealand'). Because there is no licence allowing reuse, the dataset is NOT stored in this repository; only the deep-link above is published. tools/howtovote_voting_places.py can normalise the file if the Commission confirms reuse terms (enquiries@elections.govt.nz). For 2023 the Commission published a 'voting place coordinates' CSV on the results archive (archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/statistics/) marked 'approximate only', again with no licence stated. The Commission announced the 2026 voting places on 7 October 2026 ('about 3 weeks before election day' is its stated practice). Hours and places can still change, so always check the finder before travelling.

## Contacts

- **Electoral commission freephone:** 0800 36 76 56 (free, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week; enrolment questions, finding a voting place, help to vote)
- **From overseas:** +64 9 909 4182 (international call rates may apply)
- **Text for an enrolment form:** Text your name and address to 3676 (free) and a form is posted to you
- **Enrolment email:** enrol@vote.nz (to return a scanned or photographed enrolment form)
- **Upload a form:** https://vote.nz/upload
- **Enrol or check online:** https://vote.nz/enrolling/enrol-or-update/enrol-or-update-online (needs a NZ driver licence, NZ passport or RealMe verified identity)
- **Post:** Electoral Commission, FREEPOST 2 ENROL, PO Box 190, Wellington 6140
- **General enquiries email:** enquiries@elections.govt.nz (questions, complaints about election advertising or misleading voting information)
- **Overseas voting:** overseas@vote.nz
- **Remote voting:** remote@vote.nz (DOC islands, offshore installations, vessels)
- **Telephone dictation:** 0800 028 028 within NZ (option 1 to register, option 2 to vote); +64 4 471 2000 from overseas
- **Electorate managers:** https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/contact-your-electorate-manager (name, email and phone for each electorate; use this if you can't get to a voting place)
- **Voting place finder:** https://map.vote.nz
- **Official results:** https://electionresults.govt.nz

## What we could not verify

- Official slogan of the Commission's misinformation campaign (release title is 'Take a moment before you share information'; 'Think before you share' is Waatea News' headline).
- Access 2026 'Quick guide to accessible voting services' PDF and the NZSL resources page: blocked by bot protection; summarised from the Access 2026 web page, Easy Read page and the telephone dictation page.
- Parliament.nz 'Election 2026 timeline' and DPMC Cabinet Office circular CO (26) 5 on post-election procedures: blocked; government-formation timing sourced instead to vote.nz, RNZ's The House and the Constitution Act 1986.
- Date of the Electoral Amendment Act's third reading: Ministry of Justice says 16 December 2025; a web-search summary of RNZ gave 17 December. We use the Ministry's date. Royal assent 19 December 2025 and commencement 20 December 2025 are consistent across the Ministry, the consolidated Act and Wikipedia.
- Whether the enrolment 'hub drop-off' is accepted right up to midnight 25 October: the Commission says forms can be dropped at hubs 'by 25 October'; hub hours vary (check vote.nz/enrolling/get-help-to-enrol/enrolment-in-your-community).
- Licence for the Commission's voting-place data: none found; treated as not reusable (see voting_places).
- electionresults.govt.nz itself could not be loaded from this environment (bot protection); the address is the one the Commission's key dates page links to for results.

*Raw sources: raw/howtovote/ (HTML of each Commission page as fetched 23 Oct 2026, text extracts in raw/howtovote/txt/, the consolidated Electoral Act 1993 as at 1 Jan 2026 and Constitution Act 1986 PDFs from legislation.govt.nz, and the Commission's 'Rules once voting starts' PDF).*

*Ballot Book NZ is independent and non-partisan. This page tells you how to vote, not who to vote for. See [docs/EDITORIAL_STANDARDS.md](../docs/EDITORIAL_STANDARDS.md).*

# On this day in New Zealand politics

One to three events from New Zealand's political and constitutional history for every day of the year, written in plain English. Data: [`data/onthisday.json`](../data/onthisday.json). Each entry links to the Wikipedia article used to check the date (Wikipedia is a finding aid; its articles cite the primary sources). Each day also links to NZHistory's own "Today in history" page (Ministry for Culture and Heritage, text CC BY-NC 3.0 NZ as reported; see licence notes in the JSON). Entries marked *approx.* are filed on a nearby day because no political event was found for that date; the exact date is given.

## January

### 1 January

- **1951 — Parliament becomes a single chamber** The Legislative Council, New Zealand's appointed upper house, ceased to exist on this day. Since then Parliament has had only one chamber, the House of Representatives. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Legislative_Council)
- **1987 — Constitution Act comes into force** The Constitution Act 1986 took effect. It brought together the main rules on the Sovereign, the Governor-General, Parliament and the courts, and ended the United Kingdom's power to make laws for New Zealand. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Act_1986)
- **2004 — Supreme Court of New Zealand established** New Zealand's own final court of appeal came into being, replacing appeals to the Privy Council in London. It heard its first case on 1 July 2004. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/1/1>

### 2 January

- **1877 — Provinces abolished** *(approx. — exact date 1877-01-01)* New Zealand's provincial governments formally ceased to exist, leaving a single central Parliament and local councils. The Abolition of Provinces Act had been passed in 1875. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Government)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/2/1>

### 3 January

- **1840 — Survey ship arrives for Wellington settlement** The New Zealand Company's survey ship Cuba reached Port Nicholson (Wellington) to prepare for organised British settlement, weeks before the Treaty of Waitangi was signed. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/3/1>

### 4 January

- **1876 — Māori electorates vote in the 1875-76 election** Polling in the four Māori electorates was held on 4 and 15 January 1876, as part of a general election spread over several weeks. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/4/1>

### 5 January

- **1977 — Bastion Point occupation begins** Ngāti Whātua and supporters began occupying Takaparawhau (Bastion Point) in Auckland to stop a housing development on former tribal land. The occupation lasted 506 days. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastion_Point)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/5/1>

### 6 January

- **1876 — George Grey wins the Thames seat** Former governor Sir George Grey topped the poll in Thames during the 1875-76 general election. He became premier in 1877. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Grey)
- **1923 — Birth of Norman Kirk** Norman Kirk, who led Labour to victory in 1972 and died in office in 1974, was born in Waimate. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Kirk) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/6/1>

### 7 January

- **1963 — Northern Maori MP dies** Tāpihana Paikea, Labour MP for Northern Maori, died. Matiu Rata won the by-election in March and later founded Mana Motuhake. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1963_Northern_Maori_by-election) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2018 — Death of Jim Anderton** Jim Anderton, founder of NewLabour, the Alliance and the Progressive Party and deputy prime minister from 1999 to 2002, died aged 79. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Anderton) Related: [alliance](../parties/alliance/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/7/1>

### 8 January

- **1918 — Southern Maori MP dies in office** Taare Parata, the Liberal MP for Southern Maori, died, leading to a by-election in the seat later that year. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/8/1>

### 9 January

- **1932 — Birth of Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan** Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan, MP for Southern Maori from 1967 to 1996 and the first Māori woman to serve as a Cabinet minister, was born. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whetu_Tirikatene-Sullivan) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **1976 — Former Speaker Stan Whitehead dies** Sir Stanley Whitehead, Labour MP for Nelson and a former Speaker, died in office, forcing a by-election in Nelson. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_New_Zealand_general_election) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/9/1>

### 10 January

- **1953 — Social Credit Political League founded** The Social Credit Political League was set up, growing out of an earlier monetary-reform movement. It won its first seat in 1966 and became the main third party of the 1970s and early 1980s. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Credit_Party_%28New_Zealand%29) Related: [social-credit](../parties/social-credit/README.md).
- **2024 — Waikato-Tainui files Tribunal claim over section 7AA** The iwi lodged a Waitangi Tribunal claim challenging the Government's plan to repeal section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/10/1>

### 11 January

- **1912 — New Zealand coat of arms gazetted** The royal warrant granting New Zealand its own coat of arms was published in the New Zealand Gazette. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/11/1>

### 12 January

- **1954 — The Queen opens Parliament in person** Queen Elizabeth II opened a special session of Parliament in Wellington during her first tour, the first time a reigning monarch had done so in New Zealand. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953%E2%80%931954_royal_tour_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/12/1>

### 13 January

- **1997 — Birth of the Māori Queen** Ngā Wai hono i te pō, who became Māori Queen in 2024 as head of the Kīngitanga, was born. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nga_wai_hono_i_te_po)
- **2025 — Trade deal with the United Arab Emirates signed** Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Trade Minister Todd McClay signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement with the United Arab Emirates. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [todd-mcclay](../parties/national/people/todd-mcclay/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/13/1>

### 14 January

- **1840 — Hobson sworn in as Lieutenant-Governor** William Hobson took his oath as Lieutenant-Governor of New Zealand in Sydney before sailing to the Bay of Islands to seek a treaty with Māori chiefs. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/14/1>

### 15 January

- **1871 — Māori electorates vote in the 1871 election** Elections in the four Māori electorates were held on 1 and 15 January 1871, during the general election for the 5th Parliament. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- **2014 — Kim Dotcom announces the Internet Party** Internet entrepreneur Kim Dotcom announced he would form a political party. The Internet Party later allied with Mana for the 2014 election. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Party_%28New_Zealand%29) Related: [internet-party](../parties/internet-party/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/15/1>

### 16 January

- **1894 — First woman mayor in the British Empire** Elizabeth Yates was sworn in as Mayor of Onehunga, the first woman to hold a mayoralty anywhere in the British Empire. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_New_Zealand)
- **2024 — Independent Electoral Review reports** The Ministry of Justice published the final report of the Independent Electoral Review, which recommended changes such as lowering the party-vote threshold. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_reform_in_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/16/1>

### 17 January

- **1951 — Walter Nash becomes Labour leader** Walter Nash became Leader of the Opposition after the death of Peter Fraser. He led Labour back into government in 1957. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/29th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/17/1>

### 18 January

- **2010 — Supreme Court building opened** Prince William formally opened the new Supreme Court building in Wellington. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/18/1>

### 19 January

- **2023 — Jacinda Ardern announces her resignation** Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced she would step down as Labour leader and prime minister, saying she no longer had enough in the tank. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md), [jacinda-ardern](../parties/labour/people/jacinda-ardern/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/19/1>

### 20 January

- **1883 — Governor Jervois takes office** Sir William Jervois became Governor of New Zealand. Governors at this time still played a real part in politics. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/20/1>

### 21 January

- **1891 — Atkinson's last-minute appointments** *(approx. — exact date 1891-01-22)* Outgoing Premier Harry Atkinson arranged appointments to the Legislative Council around 20-22 January 1891, days before the Liberals took office. Critics said it stacked the upper house. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/21/1>

### 22 January

- **1840 — First New Zealand Company settlers arrive** The Aurora, the first New Zealand Company ship carrying immigrants, arrived at Port Nicholson (Wellington). [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- **2023 — Chris Hipkins confirmed as Labour leader** The Labour caucus confirmed Chris Hipkins as party leader, making him prime minister-designate after Jacinda Ardern's resignation. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md), [chris-hipkins](../parties/labour/people/chris-hipkins/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/22/1>

### 23 January

- **1891 — Parliament meets to decide who governs** The 11th Parliament opened after the 1890 election. The next day the Liberals under John Ballance took office. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/23/1>

### 24 January

- **1891 — First Liberal government takes office** John Ballance's Liberal ministry took office. It is usually counted as New Zealand's first organised party government and stayed in power until 1912. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Government_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/24/1>

### 25 January

- **1873 — Birth of T. W. Rātana** Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana, founder of the Rātana movement, was born. His birthday is still marked each year at Rātana Pā, where political leaders gather before Waitangi Day. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._W._Ratana)
- **2023 — Chris Hipkins sworn in as prime minister** Chris Hipkins was sworn in as New Zealand's 41st prime minister, with Carmel Sepuloni as deputy prime minister, the first person of Pacific descent in that role. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md), [chris-hipkins](../parties/labour/people/chris-hipkins/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/25/1>

### 26 January

- **2012 — 'Teapot tape' leaked** A recording of a 2011 campaign conversation between John Key and ACT's John Banks, made in an Auckland cafe, was published online after months of legal argument. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_tape_scandal) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [john-key](../parties/national/people/john-key/README.md).
- **2024 — Plan to lower voting age dropped** The Government confirmed it would not continue the previous government's bill to lower the voting age for local elections to 16. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make_It_16_Incorporated_v_Attorney-General) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [simeon-brown](../parties/national/people/simeon-brown/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/26/1>

### 27 January

- **2022 — Raf Manji becomes TOP leader** Former Christchurch city councillor Raf Manji was named leader of The Opportunities Party. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_Party_%28New_Zealand%29) Related: [opportunity](../parties/opportunity/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/27/1>

### 28 January

- **2014 — Peter Dunne returns as a minister** Peter Dunne was reappointed to the Executive as Minister of Internal Affairs, months after resigning over a leak inquiry. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Dunne) Related: [united-future](../parties/united-future/README.md), [peter-dunne](../parties/united-future/people/peter-dunne/README.md).
- **2020 — Election date announced** Jacinda Ardern announced that the 2020 general election would be held on 19 September. It was later postponed to 17 October because of COVID-19. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_New_Zealand_general_election) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md), [jacinda-ardern](../parties/labour/people/jacinda-ardern/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/28/1>

### 29 January

- **1840 — Hobson arrives in the Bay of Islands** Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson reached the Bay of Islands aboard HMS Herald, eight days before the Treaty of Waitangi was signed. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/29/1>

### 30 January

- **1840 — Hobson reads his proclamations** At Kororāreka (Russell) Hobson read proclamations announcing his authority and that land purchases from Māori would need Crown approval. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- **2015 — Mike Sabin resigns, triggering Northland by-election** National MP Mike Sabin resigned from Parliament. Winston Peters won the resulting Northland by-election in March. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_First) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [matt-king](../parties/national/people/matt-king/README.md).
- **2025 — Taranaki Maunga redress law passed** Parliament passed the Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Act, giving the mountain legal personhood and settling Treaty claims. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/30/1>

### 31 January

- **1951 — Wage order before the waterfront dispute** The Arbitration Court issued a general wage order raising wages 15 percent. Watersiders' demands for the same rise helped trigger the 1951 waterfront dispute. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_New_Zealand_waterfront_dispute)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/31/1>

## February

### 1 February

- **2021 — Move to end Māori ward polls announced** Local Government Minister Nanaia Mahuta announced a bill to remove the rules letting a public poll overturn a council's decision to set up Māori wards. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendums_in_New_Zealand) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md), [nanaia-mahuta](../parties/labour/people/nanaia-mahuta/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/1/2>

### 2 February

- **2020 — Bridges rules out New Zealand First** National leader Simon Bridges said National would not form a coalition with New Zealand First after the 2020 election. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_New_Zealand_general_election) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [simon-bridges](../parties/national/people/simon-bridges/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/2/2>

### 3 February

- **2021 — Government approves first COVID-19 vaccine** The Government formally approved the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine for use in New Zealand. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_New_Zealand) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/3/2>

### 4 February

- **1907 — Death of Tohu Kākahi** Tohu Kākahi, one of the two prophet leaders of the Parihaka community in Taranaki, died. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parihaka)
- **1985 — USS Buchanan turned away** The Lange government declined a visit by the US warship USS Buchanan because the United States would not say whether it carried nuclear weapons. The decision strained the ANZUS alliance. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_nuclear-free_zone) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2016 — Trans-Pacific Partnership signed in Auckland** Trade ministers from twelve countries signed the TPP agreement at SkyCity in Auckland, amid protests outside. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Pacific_Partnership) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/4/2>

### 5 February

- **1840 — Chiefs debate the Treaty at Waitangi** Hobson met Māori chiefs at James Busby's house at Waitangi, where the proposed treaty was read out and debated for hours. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/5/2>

### 6 February

- **1840 — Treaty of Waitangi signed** About 40 chiefs signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi at Waitangi with William Hobson for the Crown. Copies were later taken around the country for more signatures. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi)
- **1934 — Waitangi Treaty grounds gifted to the nation** Governor-General Lord Bledisloe's gift of the Treaty House and grounds at Waitangi was formally marked at a large gathering. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitangi_Day)
- **1974 — First New Zealand Day holiday** 6 February became a national public holiday for the first time, under the New Zealand Day Act 1973. It was renamed Waitangi Day in 1976. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitangi_Day)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/6/2>

### 7 February

- **1972 — Holyoake steps down; Marshall becomes PM** Keith Holyoake resigned after more than eleven years as prime minister. Jack Marshall succeeded him, but lost the election later that year. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- **2024 — ACT launches Treaty Principles Bill campaign** ACT began a public campaign for its Treaty Principles Bill, which aimed to define the Treaty's principles in law. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_Principles_Bill) Related: [act](../parties/act/README.md), [david-seymour](../parties/act/people/david-seymour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/7/2>

### 8 February

- **1861 — MP killed in the Taranaki war** Thomas King, MP for Grey and Bell, was killed during fighting in Taranaki. Harry Atkinson, a future premier, took the seat. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- **2012 — Kiwi Party deregistered** The Kiwi Party asked to be deregistered and merged into the Conservative Party. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kiwi_Party) Related: [conservative](../parties/conservative/README.md).
- **2022 — Convoy protest arrives at Parliament** A convoy of vehicles protesting against COVID-19 vaccine mandates reached Parliament, starting an occupation of its grounds that lasted 23 days. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Wellington_protest)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/8/2>

### 9 February

- **1972 — Marshall ministry takes office** The ministers of Jack Marshall's new government were sworn in, two days after Keith Holyoake stepped down. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/9/2>

### 10 February

- **2021 — Plan to replace the Resource Management Act** The Government confirmed the Resource Management Act 1991 would be replaced by three new laws. The replacement Acts were repealed by the next government. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resource_Management_Act_1991) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2022 — Police try to clear Parliament protest** Police arrested more than 120 people in an attempt to end the occupation of Parliament's grounds. The protest continued until 2 March. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Wellington_protest)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/10/2>

### 11 February

- **2003 — Donna Awatere Huata suspended from ACT caucus** ACT suspended list MP Donna Awatere Huata after fraud allegations. She was later expelled from Parliament under party-hopping law. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [act](../parties/act/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/11/2>

### 12 February

- **1918 — Wellington North by-election** The Reform candidate held Wellington North in a wartime by-election, but a strong Labour showing alarmed the governing coalition. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1918_Wellington_North_by-election)
- **2002 — Apology for the Chinese poll tax** Prime Minister Helen Clark formally apologised to Chinese New Zealanders for the poll tax imposed on Chinese immigrants from 1881. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_head_tax) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2008 — NZ First MP Brian Donnelly resigns** Brian Donnelly left Parliament to become High Commissioner to the Cook Islands and was replaced by the next person on the New Zealand First list. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [nz-first](../parties/nz-first/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/12/2>

### 13 February

- **1951 — Waterfront dispute begins** The 1951 waterfront dispute began when watersiders refused to work overtime and employers locked them out. It lasted 151 days and the Holland government used emergency powers against the union. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_New_Zealand_waterfront_dispute) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- **2012 — MMP review opens for submissions** The Electoral Commission released a consultation paper for its review of MMP, triggered by the 2011 referendum result. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_reform_in_New_Zealand)
- **2018 — Bill English announces resignation** Former prime minister Bill English announced he would step down as National Party leader and leave Parliament. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [bill-english](../parties/national/people/bill-english/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/13/2>

### 14 February

- **2021 — Auckland put into level 3 lockdown** After new community COVID-19 cases in Papatoetoe, the Government moved Auckland to alert level 3 and the rest of the country to level 2. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_New_Zealand) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2023 — National emergency declared for Cyclone Gabrielle** The Government declared a national state of emergency, only the third in New Zealand's history, as Cyclone Gabrielle hit the North Island. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclone_Gabrielle) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/14/2>

### 15 February

- **1876 — Vogel's second ministry formed** Julius Vogel returned as premier, replacing Daniel Pollen's ministry. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- **2022 — Conversion practices ban passed** Parliament passed the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Act with broad cross-party support, banning so-called conversion therapy. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/15/2>

### 16 February

- **2007 — Taito Phillip Field quits Labour** Mangere MP Taito Phillip Field left the Labour Party after being threatened with expulsion. He later founded the New Zealand Pacific Party. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/16/2>

### 17 February

- **2009 — Electoral Finance Act repealed** Parliament repealed the Electoral Finance Act 2007 by 112 votes to 9. Only the Greens opposed the repeal. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Finance_Act_2007) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- **2021 — Pike River agency ends plan to go further into mine** The Pike River Recovery Agency abandoned plans to go beyond a rockfall in the mine, after a long political campaign by the families of the 29 men killed in 2010. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_River_Mine_disaster)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/17/2>

- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/11/12>

### 12 December

- **1957 — Walter Nash becomes prime minister** Walter Nash was sworn in as prime minister of the Second Labour Government, which lasted a single term. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **1975 — Muldoon becomes prime minister** Robert Muldoon was sworn in as prime minister after National's 1975 landslide. He held office until 1984. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- **2016 — Bill English becomes prime minister** Bill English was sworn in as prime minister, with Paula Bennett as deputy, following John Key's resignation. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/51st_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [bill-english](../parties/national/people/bill-english/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/12/12>

### 13 December

- **1949 — First National government takes office** Sidney Holland was sworn in as prime minister, the first from the National Party. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- **1986 — Constitution Act 1986 passed** Parliament unanimously passed the Constitution Act, which replaced the 1852 Act and tidied up New Zealand's constitutional rules. It took effect on 1 January 1987. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Act_1986)
- **2011 — David Shearer becomes Labour leader** David Shearer took over as Labour leader after Phil Goff's resignation, defeating David Cunliffe in a caucus vote. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md), [david-shearer](../parties/labour/people/david-shearer/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/13/12>

### 14 December

- **2023 — Fair Pay Agreements repealed** The coalition government repealed the Fair Pay Agreements system for sector-wide bargaining introduced by Labour in 2022. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_National_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [brooke-van-velden](../parties/national/people/brooke-van-velden/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/14/12>

### 15 December

- **2006 — Georgina Beyer announces retirement** Georgina Beyer, the world's first openly transgender MP, announced she would leave Parliament. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2021 — Housing intensification law passed** Parliament passed the Resource Management (Enabling Housing Supply) Amendment Act, agreed between Labour and National, allowing three homes of three storeys on most urban sites. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/15/12>

### 16 December

- **1986 — Māori Loans Affair exposed** Opposition MP Winston Peters revealed that officials had sought an unauthorised overseas loan for Māori development, embarrassing the Lange government. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Labour_Government_of_New_Zealand) Related: [nz-first](../parties/nz-first/README.md), [winston-peters](../parties/nz-first/people/winston-peters/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/16/12>

### 17 December

- **1919 — General election and liquor referendum** Voters re-elected William Massey's Reform government and voted in a referendum that narrowly kept the sale of alcohol legal. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1919_New_Zealand_general_election)
- **1991 — Muldoon leaves Parliament** Former prime minister Sir Robert Muldoon resigned as MP for Tamaki after 31 years, triggering a by-election. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/43rd_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- **2018 — Medicinal cannabis law passed** The Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Amendment Act received royal assent, allowing wider access to medicinal cannabis products. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/17/12>

### 18 December

- **2007 — Electoral Finance Bill passes** Parliament passed the Electoral Finance Bill 63 votes to 57 after months of protest. It was signed into law the next day and repealed in 2009. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Finance_Act_2007) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2018 — Cannabis referendum announced** The Government announced a referendum on legalising recreational cannabis, held with the 2020 election. Voters narrowly rejected the proposal. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_New_Zealand) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- **2019 — Rua Kēnana pardoned** Parliament passed a law pardoning the Tūhoe prophet Rua Kēnana, who was arrested in a 1916 police raid, as part of a Treaty settlement. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rua_K%C4%93nana_Hepetipa) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/18/12>

### 19 December

- **2007 — Electoral Finance Act signed into law** The Governor-General signed the Electoral Finance Act, tightening rules on election spending and third-party advertising. It was repealed in 2009. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Finance_Act_2007) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/19/12>

### 20 December

- **1875 — General election of 1875-76 begins** Polling began in a general election spread over six weeks, the last before the provinces were abolished. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- **1893 — Māori electorates vote in the 1893 election** Polling in the four Māori electorates was held three weeks after the general electorates, with Māori women voting for the first time. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_New_Zealand)
- **2011 — 50th Parliament sworn in** Members of the 50th Parliament were sworn in and Lockwood Smith was re-elected Speaker. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_New_Zealand_Parliament)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/20/12>

### 21 December

- **2019 — Gun buy-back ends** The six-month firearms buy-back that followed the Christchurch attacks closed, with more than 56,000 prohibited firearms handed in. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch_mosque_shootings) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/21/12>

### 22 December

- **1875 — George Grey elected for Auckland** Former governor Sir George Grey was declared elected unopposed in the two-member City of Auckland seat during the 1875-76 general election. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Grey)
- **1999 — Party-hopping bill introduced** The new Labour-Alliance government introduced the Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Bill to stop MPs who leave their party keeping their seats. It became law in 2001. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_%28Integrity%29_Amendment_Acts) Related: [labour](../parties/labour/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/22/12>

### 23 December

- **1953 — The Queen arrives in New Zealand** Queen Elizabeth II arrived in Auckland, the first reigning monarch to visit New Zealand, for a tour that included opening Parliament. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953%E2%80%931954_royal_tour_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/23/12>

### 24 December

- **1977 — Death of Speaker Roy Jack** Sir Roy Jack, Speaker of the House, died in office. Richard Harrison replaced him. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/38th_New_Zealand_Parliament) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/24/12>

### 25 December

- **1921 — Tūrangawaewae marae's first hui** The first gathering was held at Tūrangawaewae in Ngāruawāhia, which Te Puea Hērangi developed as the home of the Kīngitanga, the Māori King movement. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_King_movement)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/25/12>

### 26 December

- **1865 — Moutoa monument unveiled in Whanganui** A monument to Māori who fought for the Crown at Moutoa Island was unveiled at what is now Pākaitore (Moutoa Gardens), later the site of a 79-day occupation in 1995. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moutoa_Gardens)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/26/12>

### 27 December

- **1974 — Birth of Geoff Simmons** Geoff Simmons, economist and leader of The Opportunities Party from 2018 to 2022, was born. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Simmons) Related: [opportunity](../parties/opportunity/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/27/12>

### 28 December

- **1859 — Christchurch MP resigns** Richard Packer resigned as MP for the Town of Christchurch, leading to a by-election won by Henry Sewell, New Zealand's first premier. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_Town_of_Christchurch_by-election)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/28/12>

### 29 December

- **1973 — Birth of Marama Davidson** Marama Davidson, Green Party co-leader since 2018, was born. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marama_Davidson) Related: [green](../parties/green/README.md), [marama-davidson](../parties/green/people/marama-davidson/README.md).
- **2023 — Death of Sir Michael Hardie Boys** Sir Michael Hardie Boys, Governor-General from 1996 to 2001 and the first to oversee government formation under MMP, died aged 92. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Hardie_Boys)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/29/12>

### 30 December

- **1953 — The Queen visits Tūrangawaewae** Queen Elizabeth II made a brief visit to Tūrangawaewae marae, hosted by the Māori King Korokī, during her first tour of New Zealand. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_King_movement)
- **1961 — Birth of Bill English** Bill English, prime minister from 2016 to 2017 and Minister of Finance from 2008 to 2016, was born in Lumsden, Southland. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_English) Related: [national](../parties/national/README.md), [bill-english](../parties/national/people/bill-english/README.md).
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/30/12>

### 31 December

- **1853 — George Grey's first term as Governor ends** Sir George Grey left office after eight years as Governor, having overseen the Constitution Act that created Parliament. [[source]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors-general_of_New_Zealand)
- NZHistory for this day: <https://nzhistory.govt.nz/timeline/31/12>

# "Find your match" quiz (v2): what it measures and how

Data: [`data/guide/quiz2.json`](../data/guide/quiz2.json) (version `2026-10-v2`, positions frozen 2026-10-23). Built by `tools/quiz2_reconcile.py` from two independent codings, [`quiz2-coder-a.json`](../data/guide/quiz2-coder-a.json) and [`quiz2-coder-b.json`](../data/guide/quiz2-coder-b.json); the reconciliation log is [`raw/quiz2/RECONCILIATION.md`](../raw/quiz2/RECONCILIATION.md). The design rationale and literature review are in [`quiz-research.md`](quiz-research.md). This page replaces the v1 method page (45 concrete-instrument statements, single coder); v1 data remains in `data/guide/quiz.json` for comparison.

The quiz shows how close each party's **public record** is to your answers on 30 statements. It is a conversation starter, not voting advice: it ignores competence, trust, leadership, coalition arithmetic and how much weight parties themselves put on each issue.

## 1. What the quiz measures

Six dimensions, chosen from the Chapel Hill Expert Survey structure and New Zealand Election Study findings (research §2). Statement counts deliberately over-weight the economy (the most salient issue block in 2026 polling) and under-weight openness and democracy, where there are fewer live partisan divisions.

| Code | Dimension | Pole A | Pole B | Statements |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| E | State and market | active, redistributive state | lower taxes, markets, individual responsibility | 7 |
| S | Social order and personal freedom | personal freedom, social liberalism | order, tradition, tougher justice | 6 |
| T | Te Tiriti and biculturalism | partnership, Māori-specific arrangements | one law for all, uniform treatment | 6 |
| V | Environment and development | protect environment, pay for emissions | growth, extraction, faster approvals | 5 |
| O | Openness | open, pluralist, independent | fewer migrants, assimilation, traditional alliances | 3 |
| D | Democracy and power | direct democracy, limits on money, local autonomy | representative decision-making, central control | 3 |

## 2. Statement design and sources

Every statement follows ten rules (research §3.1): one principle and, where a widely acknowledged cost exists, one "even if" cost; no numbers, dates, dollar figures, Act, programme, party or leader names; affirmative wording; balanced direction within each dimension; at least two parliamentary parties codeable at opposite signs; prospective; answerable without background knowledge; a five-point scale plus a separate "no opinion / skip"; an optional importance pass (×0.5 / ×1 / ×2); and, where a validated NZES or CHES item exists, adapted from it. A regex check at build time asserts that no statement text contains a party, leader, Act or scheme name; it passes for all 30.

Polarity records which pole agreement moves toward: `+A` means agreeing places you at pole A, `+B` at pole B. Sixteen items are worded toward A and fourteen toward B (E 3/4, S 3/3, T 3/3, V 3/2, O 1/2, D 3/0); the D block is skewed and is flagged for rewording in a future version.
